title: VIII. The Evidence Of The Witnesses. The Babe
paragraphs: The questioning of the witnesses began. But we won't keep telling the story in the same detail as before. So we won't dwell on how Nikolay Parfenovitch reminded every witness that he had to testify truthfully and in good conscience, and that he would later have to repeat his testimony under oath, or on how each witness had to sign the transcript of his evidence, and so on. We'll only note that the questioning centered mainly on the matter of the three thousand roubles — that is, whether the sum Mitya spent here at Mokroe the first time, a month earlier, had been three thousand or fifteen hundred. And again, had he spent three thousand or fifteen hundred yesterday? Unfortunately, everyone's testimony turned out to be against Mitya. Not one witness spoke in his favor, and some introduced new, almost devastating facts that contradicted Mitya's own account.

The first witness questioned was Trifon Borissovitch. He wasn't in the least intimidated standing before the lawyers. On the contrary, he had an air of stern, severe indignation toward the accused, which gave him a look of honesty and personal dignity. He spoke little, and cautiously, waited to be asked, and answered precisely and deliberately. Firmly and without hesitation he testified that the sum spent a month before could not have been less than three thousand — that every peasant around here would confirm hearing that figure from Dmitri Fyodorovitch's own mouth. "What a pile of money he threw away on the gypsy girls alone! I'd guess he wasted a thousand on them alone."
"I don't believe I gave them five hundred," was Mitya's gloomy comment on this. "It's a pity I didn't count the money at the time, but I was drunk...."
Mitya sat sideways, his back to the curtains. He listened gloomily, with a weary, melancholy air, as though he wanted to say:
"Say whatever you like. It makes no difference now."

"More than a thousand went on them, Dmitri Fyodorovitch," Trifon Borissovitch retorted firmly. "You scattered it around at random and they snatched it up. A thieving, rascally lot they were, horse-stealers — they've been chased out of here since, or maybe they'd testify themselves how much they got out of you. I saw the sum in your hands myself — I didn't count it, you wouldn't let me, that's true enough — but by the look of it I'd say it was far more than fifteen hundred ... fifteen hundred, indeed! We've handled money too. We know how to judge amounts...."
As for the sum spent yesterday, he insisted that Dmitri Fyodorovitch had told him, the moment he arrived, that he'd brought three thousand with him.
"Come now, is that really so, Trifon Borissovitch?" Mitya replied. "Surely I didn't say so flatly that I'd brought three thousand?"

"You did say so, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. You said it in front of Andrey. Andrey's still here — send for him. And in the hall, when you were treating the chorus, you shouted outright that you'd leave your sixth thousand here — meaning, we're to understand, on top of what you spent before. Stepan and Semyon heard it, and Pyotr Fomitch Kalganov was standing right beside you at the time. Maybe he remembers it too...."

This evidence about the "sixth" thousand made an extraordinary impression on the two lawyers. They were delighted with this new way of reckoning: three and three made six — three thousand back then and three thousand now made six. That was clear enough.

They questioned all the peasants Trifon Borissovitch had named — Stepan, Semyon, the driver Andrey, and Kalganov. The peasants and the driver confirmed Trifon Borissovitch's testimony without hesitation. They noted down, with particular care, Andrey's account of the conversation he'd had with Mitya on the road: "'Where,' he says, 'am I going, Dmitri Fyodorovitch — to heaven or to hell, and will I be forgiven in the next world or not?'"
The psychologically minded Ippolit Kirillovitch heard this with a subtle smile, and ended by recommending that these remarks about where Dmitri Fyodorovitch was headed be "included in the record."

Kalganov, when called, came in reluctantly, scowling and ill-tempered, and spoke to the lawyers as if he'd never met them before in his life, though they were acquaintances he'd been seeing daily for a long time. He began by saying "he knew nothing about it and didn't want to." But it turned out he had heard of the "sixth" thousand, and he admitted he'd been standing close by at the time. As far as he could tell, he "didn't know" how much money Mitya had had in his hands. He confirmed that the Poles had cheated at cards. Under repeated questioning he stated that after the Poles had been turned out, Mitya's standing with Agrafena Alexandrovna had definitely improved, and that she'd said she loved him. He spoke of Agrafena Alexandrovna with reserve and respect, as though she were a lady of the finest society, and never once let himself call her Grushenka. Despite the young man's obvious distaste for giving evidence, Ippolit Kirillovitch questioned him at great length, and it was only from him that he learned the full details of what made up Mitya's "romance," so to speak, that night. Mitya never once interrupted Kalganov. At last they let the young man go, and he left the room with undisguised indignation.

The Poles were questioned too. Though they had gone to bed in their room, they hadn't slept at all that night, and when the police officers arrived they hastily dressed and made themselves ready, realizing they'd certainly be sent for. They gave their evidence with dignity, though not without some unease. The smaller Pole turned out to be a retired official of the twelfth class who had served as a veterinary surgeon in Siberia. His name was Mussyalovitch. Pan Vrublevsky turned out to be an uncertified dentist. Although Nikolay Parfenovitch directed his questions at them, they both addressed their answers to Mihail Makarovitch, who was standing off to one side, mistaking him in their ignorance for the most important person in charge, and calling him "Pan Colonel" at every turn. Only after several corrections from Mihail Makarovitch himself did they grasp that they were to address Nikolay Parfenovitch alone. It turned out they could speak quite correct Russian, apart from their accent on certain words. Of his relations with Grushenka, past and present, Pan Mussyalovitch spoke proudly and warmly, so that Mitya flared up at once and declared he wouldn't allow the "scoundrel" to talk like that in his presence! Pan Mussyalovitch immediately drew attention to the word "scoundrel" and asked that it be entered in the record. Mitya seethed with rage.
"He's a scoundrel! A scoundrel! You can write that down. And write down too that, record or no record, I still say he's a scoundrel!" he cried.

Though Nikolay Parfenovitch did enter this in the record, he showed remarkably good tact and judgment in handling it. After sternly reprimanding Mitya, he cut off all further inquiry into the romantic side of the case and hurried on to what mattered. One piece of evidence given by the Poles caught the lawyers' particular interest: how, in that very room, Mitya had tried to buy off Pan Mussyalovitch, offering him three thousand roubles to give up his claims — seven hundred roubles down, and the remaining two thousand three hundred "to be paid the next day in town." He'd sworn at the time that he didn't have the whole sum with him at Mokroe, but that his money was in town. Mitya protested hotly that he hadn't said he'd definitely pay him the rest the next day in town. But Pan Vrublevsky backed up the claim, and Mitya, after thinking a moment, admitted, frowning, that it must have happened the way the Poles described — that he'd been worked up at the time and might well have said so.

The prosecutor seized on this piece of evidence at once. It seemed to establish for the prosecution (and in fact they built this very conclusion on it) that half, or a part, of the three thousand that had come into Mitya's hands might really have been left hidden somewhere in town — or even, perhaps, somewhere here at Mokroe. This would explain the fact that had so puzzled the prosecution, that only eight hundred roubles had been found on Mitya. That fact, small as it was, had until now been the one piece of evidence that told, to some degree, in Mitya's favor. Now that one piece of evidence in his favor had collapsed. When the prosecutor pressed him on where he'd have gotten the remaining two thousand three hundred roubles, since he himself had denied having more than fifteen hundred, Mitya confidently replied that he'd meant to offer the "little fellow" not money, but a formal deed transferring his rights to the village of Tchermashnya — the same rights he'd already offered Samsonov and Madame Hohlakov. The prosecutor all but smiled at the "innocence of this dodge."
"And you imagine he would have accepted such a deed as a substitute for two thousand three hundred roubles in cash?"

"He certainly would have accepted it," Mitya declared warmly. "Why, look here — he might have squeezed out not two thousand but four or six for it. He'd have set his lawyers on it, Poles and Jews, and could have gotten not three thousand but the whole property out of the old man."

Pan Mussyalovitch's testimony was, of course, entered into the record in the fullest detail. Then they let the Poles go. The matter of the card-cheating was barely touched on. Nikolay Parfenovitch was too pleased with them as it was and didn't want to bother them over trifles — besides, it was nothing but a foolish, drunken quarrel over cards. There had been plenty of drinking and disorder that night.... So the two hundred roubles stayed in the Poles' pockets.

Then old Maximov was summoned. He came in timidly, with small steps, looking disheveled and downcast. All this time he'd been taking shelter downstairs with Grushenka, sitting mutely beside her, and "now and then he'd start blubbering over her and wiping his eyes with a blue checked handkerchief," as Mihail Makarovitch described it afterward. So much so that she herself had started trying to calm and comfort him. The old man confessed right away that he'd done wrong, that he'd borrowed "ten roubles in my poverty" from Dmitri Fyodorovitch, and that he was ready to pay it back. To Nikolay Parfenovitch's direct question — whether he'd noticed how much money Dmitri Fyodorovitch was holding, since he must have been able to see the sum better than anyone when he took the note from him — Maximov declared, quite positively, that there had been twenty thousand.
"Have you ever seen as much as twenty thousand before, then?" Nikolay Parfenovitch asked, with a smile.

"To be sure I have — not twenty, but seven, when my wife mortgaged my little property. She only let me look at it from a distance, boasting of it to me. It was a very thick bundle, all rainbow-colored notes. And Dmitri Fyodorovitch's were all rainbow-colored too...."

He wasn't kept long. At last it was Grushenka's turn. Nikolay Parfenovitch was visibly worried about the effect her appearance might have on Mitya, and he murmured a few words of caution to him, but Mitya bowed his head in silence, letting him understand "that he wouldn't make a scene." Mihail Makarovitch himself led Grushenka in. She came in with a stern, gloomy face that looked almost composed, and sat quietly in the chair Nikolay Parfenovitch offered her. She was very pale, seemed to be cold, and wrapped herself tightly in her magnificent black shawl. She was running a slight fever — the first symptom of the long illness that followed that night. Her grave manner, her direct, earnest gaze and quiet bearing made a very favorable impression on everyone. Nikolay Parfenovitch was even a little "charmed." He admitted afterward, talking about it, that only then had he seen "how handsome the woman was," for though he'd seen her several times before, he'd always thought of her as something of a "provincial hetaira." "She has the manners of the best society," he said enthusiastically, gossiping about her in a circle of ladies. But this was met with real indignation from the ladies, who at once called him a "naughty man," to his great satisfaction.

As she entered the room, Grushenka only glanced at Mitya for an instant; he looked at her uneasily. But her face reassured him at once. After the usual preliminary inquiries and warnings, Nikolay Parfenovitch asked her, hesitating slightly but keeping his most courteous manner, what her relations were with the retired lieutenant Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov. To this Grushenka replied firmly and quietly:

"He was an acquaintance. He came to see me as an acquaintance over the last month." To further probing questions she answered plainly and with complete frankness that, though "at times" she'd found him attractive, she hadn't loved him, but had won his heart, as well as his old father's, "out of my own nasty spite" — that she'd seen Mitya was very jealous of Fyodor Pavlovitch and everyone else, but that had only amused her. She'd never meant to go to Fyodor Pavlovitch — she'd simply been laughing at him. "I had no thoughts for either of them this whole last month. I was waiting for another man, one who'd wronged me. But I don't think," she said in conclusion, "that there's any need for you to ask about that, or for me to answer, because that's my own affair."

Nikolay Parfenovitch immediately took the hint. He again set aside the "romantic" side of the case and moved to the serious one — that is, to the question that mattered most, the three thousand roubles. Grushenka confirmed that three thousand roubles had certainly been spent on the first spree at Mokroe, and, though she hadn't counted the money herself, she'd heard it was three thousand from Dmitri Fyodorovitch's own lips.
"Did he tell you that alone, or in front of someone else, or did you only hear him mention it to others in your presence?" the prosecutor asked at once.
To which Grushenka answered that she'd heard him say so in front of other people, and had heard him say so when they were alone together.
"Did he say it to you alone once, or several times?" the prosecutor asked, and learned that he'd told Grushenka so several times.

Ippolit Kirillovitch was very pleased with this piece of evidence. Further questioning brought out that Grushenka also knew where the money had come from — that Dmitri Fyodorovitch had gotten it from Katerina Ivanovna.
"And did you never, not once, hear that the money spent a month ago wasn't three thousand but less, and that Dmitri Fyodorovitch had kept back half that sum for himself?"
"No, I never heard that," answered Grushenka.
It came out further that Mitya had, on the contrary, often told her he didn't have a farthing.
"He was always expecting to get some from his father," Grushenka said in conclusion.
"Did he ever say in front of you ... offhandedly, or in a fit of temper," Nikolay Parfenovitch put in suddenly, "that he meant to make an attempt on his father's life?"
"Ah, he did say that," Grushenka sighed.
"Once, or several times?"
"He mentioned it several times, always in anger."
"And did you believe he'd do it?"
"No, I never believed it," she answered firmly. "I had faith in his noble heart."
"Gentlemen, allow me," Mitya suddenly cried, "allow me to say one word to Agrafena Alexandrovna, in front of you all."
"You may speak," Nikolay Parfenovitch agreed.
"Agrafena Alexandrovna!" Mitya got up from his chair. "Have faith in God and in me. I am not guilty of my father's murder!"

Having said these words, Mitya sat back down on his chair. Grushenka stood up and crossed herself devoutly before the icon. "Thanks be to Thee, O Lord," she said, her voice thrilled with emotion, and, still standing, she turned to Nikolay Parfenovitch and added:

"Since he's said that now, believe it! I know him. He'll say anything as a joke, or out of stubbornness, but he'll never deceive you against his conscience. He's telling the whole truth — you can believe it."
"Thank you, Agrafena Alexandrovna, you've given me fresh courage," Mitya answered in a trembling voice.

As for the money spent the day before, she said she didn't know what sum it was, but had heard him tell several people that he had three thousand on him. Asked where he'd gotten the money, she said he'd told her he'd "stolen" it from Katerina Ivanovna, and that she'd replied that he hadn't stolen it, and that he must pay the money back the next day. When the prosecutor pressed her on whether the money he'd said he'd stolen from Katerina Ivanovna was what he'd spent yesterday, or what he'd squandered here a month before, she declared he'd meant the money spent a month before, and that that was how she'd understood him.

Grushenka was finally released, and Nikolay Parfenovitch told her impulsively that she could return to town at once, and that if he could be of any help to her — with horses, say, or if she wanted an escort — he ... would be—

"I thank you sincerely," said Grushenka, bowing to him, "I'm going with this old gentleman, I'm driving him back to town with me, and in the meantime, if you'll allow me, I'll wait downstairs to hear what you decide about Dmitri Fyodorovitch."

She went out. Mitya was calm, even looking somewhat more cheerful — but only for a moment. He felt more and more weighed down by a strange physical weakness. His eyes kept closing with fatigue. The questioning of the witnesses was finally over. They moved on to a final review of the record. Mitya got up, moved from his chair to the corner by the curtain, lay down on a large chest covered with a rug, and instantly fell asleep.
He had a strange dream, entirely out of keeping with the place and the moment.

He was driving somewhere across the steppe, where he'd once been stationed long ago, and a peasant was driving him in a cart pulled by a pair of horses, through snow and sleet. He was cold — it was early November, and the snow was falling in big wet flakes that melted as soon as they touched the ground. The peasant drove him briskly; he had a fair, long beard. He wasn't an old man, somewhere around fifty, and wore a gray peasant's smock. Not far off was a village — he could see the black huts, and half of them were burned down, only the charred beams still sticking up. And as they drove in, there were peasant women lined up along the road, a great many of them, a whole row, all thin and gaunt, their faces a sort of brownish color — especially one at the edge, a tall, bony woman who looked forty but might have been only twenty, with a long, thin face. In her arms was a little baby, crying. Her breasts seemed so dried up there wasn't a drop of milk in them. And the child cried and cried, holding out its little bare arms, its little fists blue with cold.
"Why are they crying? Why are they crying?" Mitya asked, as they dashed cheerfully past.
"It's the babe," the driver answered, "the babe weeping."
And Mitya was struck by the way he said it, in his peasant fashion — "the babe" — and he liked the peasant calling it a "babe." There seemed to be more pity in it.
"But why is it weeping?" Mitya persisted stupidly. "Why are its little arms bare? Why don't they wrap it up?"
"The babe's cold, its little clothes are frozen and don't warm it."
"But why is that? Why?" foolish Mitya persisted still.
"Well, they're poor folk, burned out. They've got no bread. They're begging because they've been burned out."

"No, no," Mitya still seemed not to understand. "Tell me why those poor mothers are standing there. Why are people poor? Why is the babe poor? Why is the steppe so bare? Why don't they hug each other and kiss? Why don't they sing songs of joy? Why are they so dark with black misery? Why don't they feed the babe?"

And he felt that, senseless and unreasonable as his questions were, he still wanted to ask exactly that, and had to ask it in just that way. And he felt a passion of pity rising in his heart such as he'd never known before — that he wanted to cry, that he wanted to do something for all of them, so that the babe would weep no more, so that the dark-faced, dried-up mother wouldn't weep, so that no one would shed another tear from that moment on — and he wanted to do it at once, right away, regardless of every obstacle, with all the Karamazov recklessness.

"And I'm coming with you. I won't leave you now for the rest of my life, I'm coming with you," he heard close beside him, Grushenka's tender voice, thrilling with feeling. And his heart glowed, and he pushed forward toward the light, longing to live, to live, to go on and on, toward the new, beckoning light, and to hurry, hurry, now, at once!

"What! Where?" he exclaimed, opening his eyes and sitting up on the chest, as if he'd come back to life from a faint, smiling brightly. Nikolay Parfenovitch was standing over him, suggesting he listen to the record read aloud and sign it. Mitya guessed he'd been asleep an hour or more, but he wasn't listening to Nikolay Parfenovitch. He was suddenly struck by the fact that there was a pillow under his head — one that hadn't been there when he'd slumped back, exhausted, on the chest.
"Who put this pillow under my head? Who was so kind?" he cried, with a sort of ecstatic gratitude and tears in his voice, as though some great kindness had been shown him.

He never found out who this kind soul had been — maybe one of the peasant witnesses, or Nikolay Parfenovitch's little secretary, had thought, out of compassion, to put a pillow under his head — but his whole soul was trembling with tears. He went to the table and said he'd sign whatever they liked.
"I've had a good dream, gentlemen," he said in a strange voice, a new light, like joy, on his face.

title: IX. They Carry Mitya Away
paragraphs: Once the record had been signed, Nikolay Parfenovitch turned solemnly to the prisoner and read him the "Committal," stating that in such-and-such a year, on such-and-such a day, in such-and-such a place, the investigating lawyer of such-and-such a district court, having examined so-and-so (namely, Mitya), accused of this and that (all the charges were carefully spelled out), and having found that the accused, not pleading guilty to the charges against him, had offered nothing in his defense, while the witnesses so-and-so and so-and-so, and the circumstances such-and-such, testified against him — acting in accordance with such-and-such articles of the Statute Book, and so on — had ruled that, in order to prevent so-and-so (Mitya) from evading pursuit and judgment by any means, he be held in such-and-such a prison, which he hereby notifies to the accused and of which he sends a copy to the deputy prosecutor, and so on, and so on.

In short, Mitya was informed that from that moment he was a prisoner, and that he'd be driven to town at once and locked up somewhere thoroughly unpleasant. Mitya listened attentively, and only shrugged his shoulders.
"Well, gentlemen, I don't blame you. I'm ready.... I understand there's nothing else for you to do."
Nikolay Parfenovitch informed him gently that he'd be escorted at once by the rural police officer, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, who happened to be on hand....
"Wait," Mitya interrupted suddenly, and, driven by an uncontrollable urge, he addressed everyone in the room:

"Gentlemen, we're all cruel, we're all monsters, we all make people weep — mothers, and babies at the breast — but of all of us, let it be settled here, now, that I'm the lowest reptile of them all! I've sworn to reform, and every day I've done the same filthy things. I understand now that men like me need a blow — a blow of fate to catch them like a noose and bind them by force from outside. I would never, never have risen on my own! But the thunderbolt has fallen. I accept the torment of the accusation, my public shame — I want to suffer, and through suffering I'll be purified. Maybe I'll be purified, gentlemen? But listen, for the last time: I am not guilty of my father's blood. I accept my punishment, not because I killed him, but because I meant to kill him, and might really have killed him. Still, I intend to fight this out with you. I warn you of that. I'll fight it out with you to the end, and then God will decide. Goodbye, gentlemen, don't hold it against me for shouting at you during the questioning. Oh, I was such a fool then.... In another minute I'll be a prisoner, but now, for the last time, as a free man, Dmitri Karamazov offers you his hand. In saying goodbye to you, I say it to all men."

His voice shook and he stretched out his hand, but Nikolay Parfenovitch, who happened to be standing nearest him, with a sudden, almost nervous movement, hid his hands behind his back. Mitya noticed this at once and started. He let his outstretched hand drop instantly.

"The preliminary inquiry isn't over yet," Nikolay Parfenovitch faltered, somewhat embarrassed. "We'll continue it in town, and I, for my part, of course, am ready to wish you every success ... in your defense.... As a matter of fact, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, I've always been inclined to see you as, so to speak, more unfortunate than guilty. All of us here, if I may speak for everyone, are ready to recognize that you are, at bottom, a young man of honor, but one who has been carried away, alas, by certain passions to a rather excessive degree...."

By the time he finished speaking, Nikolay Parfenovitch's little figure had become positively majestic. It struck Mitya that in another minute this "boy" would take his arm, lead him to another corner, and pick up their conversation about "girls" again. But all sorts of irrelevant, inappropriate thoughts can occur even to a prisoner being led out to execution.
"Gentlemen, you're kind, you're humane — may I see her, to say goodbye for the last time?" Mitya asked.
"Certainly, but considering ... in fact, right now it's not possible except in the presence of—"
"Oh, well, if it has to be, it has to be!"
Grushenka was brought in, but the farewell was brief, said in few words, and didn't at all satisfy Nikolay Parfenovitch. Grushenka bowed low to Mitya.
"I've told you I am yours, and I will be yours. I'll follow you forever, wherever they send you. Farewell — you are innocent, though you've been your own ruin."
Her lips trembled, tears streamed from her eyes.
"Forgive me, Grusha, for my love — for ruining you too with my love."

Mitya would have said more, but he broke off and went out. He was at once surrounded by men keeping constant watch over him. At the bottom of the steps up which he'd driven with such a dash the day before, behind Andrey's three horses, two carts now stood ready. Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, a sturdy, thickset man with a lined face, was annoyed about something — some sudden mix-up. He was shouting angrily. He told Mitya to get into the cart with rather excessive gruffness.

"When I was standing him drinks in the tavern, the man had quite a different face," Mitya thought, as he climbed in. At the gates a crowd had gathered — peasants, women, drivers. Trifon Borissovitch came down the steps too. Everyone stared at Mitya.
"Forgive me as I go, good people!" Mitya shouted suddenly from the cart.
"Forgive us too!" two or three voices called back.
"Goodbye to you too, Trifon Borissovitch!"

But Trifon Borissovitch didn't even turn around. He was, perhaps, too busy. He too was shouting and fussing about something. It turned out that not everything was ready yet in the second cart, in which two constables were to accompany Mavriky Mavrikyevitch. The peasant ordered to drive the second cart was pulling on his smock, stubbornly insisting it wasn't his turn to go, but Akim's. But Akim was nowhere to be seen. They ran off to find him. The peasant kept insisting and begging them to wait.

"You see what our peasants are like, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch. No shame at all!" exclaimed Trifon Borissovitch. "Akim gave you twenty-five kopecks the day before yesterday. You've drunk it all up and now you're making a fuss. I'm simply amazed at your patience with our low peasants, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, that's all I have to say."
"But what do we need a second cart for?" Mitya put in. "Let's just go with the one, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch. I won't misbehave, I won't run off from you, old fellow. What do we need an escort for?"

"I'll trouble you, sir, to learn how to address me, if no one's taught you yet. I'm not 'old fellow' to you, and you can keep your advice to yourself!" Mavriky Mavrikyevitch snapped out savagely, as if glad of the chance to vent his temper.

Mitya fell silent. He flushed all over. A moment later he suddenly felt very cold. The rain had stopped, but the dull sky was still overcast with clouds, and a sharp wind was blowing straight into his face.
"I've caught a chill," Mitya thought, twitching his shoulders.

At last Mavriky Mavrikyevitch too climbed into the cart, sat down heavily, and, as if without noticing, squeezed Mitya into the corner. True, he was out of sorts and thoroughly disliked the task that had been dumped on him.
"Goodbye, Trifon Borissovitch!" Mitya shouted again, and felt, himself, that this time it hadn't come from good nature but involuntarily, out of resentment.
But Trifon Borissovitch stood there proudly, both hands behind his back, staring straight at Mitya with a stern, angry face, and made no reply.
"Goodbye, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, goodbye!" he suddenly heard Kalganov's voice, who'd darted out unexpectedly. Running up to the cart, he held out his hand to Mitya. He had no cap on.
Mitya just managed to seize and press his hand.
"Goodbye, dear fellow! I won't forget your generosity," he cried warmly.
But the cart moved and their hands came apart. The bell began ringing and Mitya was driven off.

Kalganov ran back, sat down in a corner, bent his head, buried his face in his hands, and burst into tears. He sat like that for a long while, crying like a little boy rather than a young man of twenty. Oh, he believed, almost without a doubt, in Mitya's guilt.
"What are these people? What can men be, after this?" he exclaimed incoherently, in bitter despondency, nearly despair. At that moment he had no desire to live at all.
"Is it worth it? Is it worth it?" the boy exclaimed in his grief.
PART IV

title: I. Kolya Krassotkin
paragraphs: It was the beginning of November. There had been a hard frost — eleven degrees Réaumur — without snow, but a little dry snow had fallen on the frozen ground overnight, and a sharp, dry wind was lifting it and blowing it along the dreary streets of our town, especially around the market square. It was a dull morning, but the snow had stopped.

Not far from the market square, close to Plotnikov's shop, stood a small house, very clean both inside and out. It belonged to Madame Krassotkin, the widow of a former provincial secretary who had been dead for fourteen years. His widow, still a nice-looking woman of thirty-two, was living in her tidy little house on her own private means. She lived in respectable seclusion; she had a gentle but fairly cheerful temperament. She'd been about eighteen when her husband died — married only a year, and had just given birth to a son. From the day of his death she had devoted herself heart and soul to raising her precious treasure, her boy Kolya. Though she'd loved him passionately for those fourteen years, he'd caused her far more suffering than happiness. She trembled and nearly fainted with terror almost every day, afraid he'd fall ill, catch cold, do something reckless, climb on a chair and fall off it, and so on and so forth. When Kolya started school, his mother threw herself into studying every subject alongside him, so she could help him and go through his lessons with him. She hurried to make friends with the teachers and their wives, even courted Kolya's schoolmates, fawning over them in hopes of sparing Kolya from being teased, laughed at, or beaten. She went so far that the boys actually started mocking him for it, taunting him as a "mama's boy."

But the boy could hold his own. He was a determined boy, "tremendously strong," as the rumor went in his class, and it soon proved true; he was agile, strong-willed, bold and enterprising by temperament. He did well at his lessons, and there was a rumor around school that he could beat the teacher, Dardanelov, at arithmetic and world history. Though he looked down on everyone, he was a good companion, not stuck-up. He accepted his schoolmates' respect as his due, but stayed friendly with them. Above all, he knew where to draw the line. He could restrain himself when he chose, and in his dealings with the teachers he never crossed that last invisible boundary past which a prank becomes an unforgivable breach of discipline. But he was as fond of mischief on every possible occasion as the smallest boy in the school — and not so much for the sake of mischief as for making a splash, inventing something striking and conspicuous. He was extremely vain. He knew how to make even his mother give in to him; he ruled her almost like a little despot. She gave in to him — oh, she'd been giving in to him for years. The one thought she couldn't bear was that her boy had no great love for her. She was always imagining Kolya was "cold" toward her, and at times, dissolving into hysterical tears, she'd reproach him for his coldness. The boy disliked this, and the more he was pressed for shows of feeling, the more he seemed to deliberately avoid them. Yet it wasn't deliberate on his part but instinctive — it was simply his nature. His mother was wrong; he was very fond of her. He only disliked "soppy sentimentality," as he put it in his schoolboy way.

There was a bookcase in the house holding a few of his father's old books. Kolya loved to read, and had gotten through several of them on his own. His mother didn't mind, and only sometimes wondered, seeing the boy stand for hours at the bookcase poring over a book instead of going out to play. And that was how Kolya came to read a few things unsuitable for his age.

Though the boy generally knew where to draw the line in his mischief, he'd lately begun playing pranks that seriously alarmed his mother. It's true there was nothing vicious in what he did, only a wild, reckless streak.

It happened that in July, during summer break, mother and son went to another district, forty-five miles away, to spend a week with a distant relation whose husband worked as an official at the railway station — the very station, nearest to our town, from which Ivan Fyodorovitch Karamazov would set off for Moscow a month later. There Kolya began by thoroughly investigating every detail connected with the railway, knowing he could impress his schoolmates back home with his newly gained knowledge. But it happened there were some other boys in the area, and he soon made friends with them. Some lived at the station, others nearby; there were six or seven of them, all between twelve and fifteen, and two came from our own town. The boys played together, and on the fourth or fifth day of Kolya's stay at the station, the foolish boys made a mad bet. Kolya, who was almost the youngest of the group and rather looked down on by the others because of it, was moved by vanity, or reckless bravado, to bet them two roubles that he'd lie down between the rails at night when the eleven o'clock train was due, and lie there without moving while the train rolled over him at full speed. True, they'd made a preliminary check beforehand, which showed it was possible to lie flat enough between the rails that the train would pass over without touching — but lying there was no joke! Kolya stoutly maintained he'd do it. At first they laughed at him, called him a little liar, a braggart, but that only spurred him on. What stung him most was that these fifteen-year-olds turned up their noses at him too, and were at first inclined to treat him as "a little kid," not fit company for them — an insult he couldn't bear.

So it was decided to go out that evening, half a mile from the station, so the train would have time to reach full speed after leaving. The boys gathered. It was a pitch-black night with no moon. At the appointed time, Kolya lay down between the rails. The five others who'd taken the bet waited in the bushes below the embankment, hearts pounding with suspense, which soon gave way to alarm and remorse. At last they heard, in the distance, the rumble of the train leaving the station. Two red lights gleamed out of the darkness; the monster roared as it approached.

"Run, run away from the rails," the boys cried to Kolya from the bushes, breathless with terror. But it was too late: the train rushed up and flew past. The boys ran to Kolya. He lay there without moving. They pulled at him, lifted him up. He suddenly got up and walked off without a word. He later explained that he'd lain there as though senseless just to frighten them, but the truth was he'd really lost consciousness, as he confessed long afterward to his mother. That's how his reputation as "a desperate character" was sealed for good. He came back to the station white as a sheet. The next day he ran a slight nervous fever, but he was in high spirits and thoroughly pleased with himself. The incident didn't become known right away, but once they returned to town it reached the school and even the teachers' ears. But then Kolya's mother rushed to plead with the teachers on her boy's behalf, and in the end Dardanelov, a respected and influential teacher, exerted himself on his behalf, and the matter was let drop.

Dardanelov was a middle-aged bachelor who had been passionately in love with Madame Krassotkin for years, and had once already, about a year before, ventured — trembling with fear and the delicacy of his feelings — to offer her, most respectfully, his hand in marriage. But she'd refused him flatly, feeling that accepting would be a betrayal of her son, though Dardanelov had, judging by certain mysterious signs, reason to believe he wasn't unwelcome to the charming but overly cautious and tender-hearted widow. Kolya's mad prank seemed to have broken the ice, and Dardanelov was rewarded for his intervention with a hint of hope. That hint, true, was a faint one, but Dardanelov was such a paragon of purity and delicacy that it was enough, for the time being, to make him perfectly happy. He was fond of the boy, though he'd have considered it beneath him to try to win him over, and he was strict and severe with him in class. Kolya, for his part, kept him at a respectful distance. He learned his lessons perfectly; he stood second in his class, was reserved with Dardanelov, and the whole class firmly believed that Kolya was so good at world history he could "beat" even Dardanelov. Kolya had indeed once asked him, "Who founded Troy?" — to which Dardanelov had given a very vague answer, gesturing toward the movements and migrations of peoples, the remoteness of the period, the mythical legends involved. But the question of who, specifically, had founded Troy, he couldn't answer, and even seemed to regard the question as idle and frivolous. But the boys stayed convinced that Dardanelov didn't know who founded Troy. Kolya had read about the founders of Troy in Smaragdov, whose history was among the books in his father's bookcase. Eventually all the boys grew curious about who had founded Troy, but Krassotkin wouldn't give away his secret, and his reputation for knowledge remained intact.

After the incident on the railway, a certain change came over Kolya's attitude toward his mother. When Anna Fyodorovna (Madame Krassotkin) learned of her son's exploit, she nearly lost her mind with horror. She suffered such terrible fits of hysterics, on and off for several days, that Kolya, genuinely alarmed at last, promised on his honor never to repeat such pranks. He swore it on his knees before the holy icon, and swore by his father's memory, at Madame Krassotkin's insistence, and the "manly" Kolya burst into tears like a boy of six. And all that day mother and son kept flinging themselves into each other's arms, sobbing. The next day Kolya woke up just as "cold" as before, but he'd grown more silent, more modest, sterner, more thoughtful.

Six weeks later, true, he got into another scrape, which even reached the ears of our Justice of the Peace — but it was a scrape of quite another sort, foolish and amusing, and he turned out not to have taken the lead in it, only to have been dragged into it. But more of that later. His mother still fretted and trembled, but the more anxious she grew, the higher Dardanelov's hopes rose. It should be noted that Kolya understood and guessed what was in Dardanelov's heart, and, of course, despised him thoroughly for his "feelings"; he'd once even been tactless enough to show this contempt in front of his mother, hinting vaguely that he knew what Dardanelov was after. But since the railway incident his behavior on this point had also changed; he never allowed himself the faintest allusion to it anymore, and began speaking more respectfully of Dardanelov in front of his mother, which the sensitive woman noticed at once with boundless gratitude. But at the slightest mention of Dardanelov by a visitor in Kolya's presence, she'd flush as pink as a rose. At such moments Kolya would either stare out the window scowling, or examine the state of his boots, or shout angrily for "Perezvon," the big, shaggy, mangy dog he'd picked up a month before, brought home, and kept indoors for some reason in secret, never showing him to any of his schoolmates. He bullied him mercilessly, teaching him all kinds of tricks, so that the poor dog howled whenever he was away at school, and whined with delight when he came in, ran about as if crazed, begged, lay down pretending to be dead, and so on — going through all the tricks he'd been taught, not at any command, but simply out of the zeal of his excited, grateful heart.

I've forgotten to mention, by the way, that Kolya Krassotkin was the boy stabbed with a penknife by the boy the reader already knows as the son of Captain Snegiryov. Ilusha had been defending his father when the schoolboys jeered at him, shouting the nickname "wisp of tow."

title: II. Children
paragraphs: So on that frosty, snowy, windy day in November, Kolya Krassotkin was sitting at home. It was Sunday, no school. It had just struck eleven, and he badly wanted to go out "on very urgent business," but he'd been left alone in charge of the house, because all its adult residents happened to be out on account of a sudden, singular event. Madame Krassotkin had let two small rooms, separated from the rest of the house by a passage, to a doctor's wife with her two small children. This lady was the same age as Anna Fyodorovna and a close friend of hers. Her husband, the doctor, had left twelve months earlier, first for Orenburg and then for Tashkent, and for the last six months she hadn't heard a word from him. If not for her friendship with Madame Krassotkin, which gave her some comfort, the abandoned lady would surely have dissolved entirely into tears. And now, to top off her troubles, Katerina, her one servant, had suddenly announced the evening before, to her mistress's amazement, that she meant to bring a child into the world before morning. It struck everyone as almost miraculous that no one had noticed it coming sooner. The astonished doctor's wife decided to move Katerina, while there was still time, to a place in town kept by a midwife for such emergencies. Since she set great store by her servant, she carried out the plan at once and stayed there looking after her. By morning, all of Madame Krassotkin's friendly sympathy and energy had been called on to help and to appeal to someone for assistance with the whole matter.

So both ladies were away from home, the Krassotkins' servant Agafya had gone off to market, and Kolya was left for the time being to protect and look after "the kids" — that is, the son and daughter of the doctor's wife, who'd been left alone. Kolya wasn't afraid to look after the house; besides, he had Perezvon, who'd been told to lie flat, without moving, under the bench in the hall. Every time Kolya, pacing back and forth through the rooms, came into the hall, the dog shook his head and gave two loud, coaxing thumps of his tail on the floor — but alas, the whistle that would release him never sounded. Kolya looked sternly at the unlucky dog, who sank back into obedient stillness. The one thing that troubled Kolya was "the kids." He looked, of course, with total scorn on Katerina's unexpected turn of events, but he was very fond of the orphaned little "kiddies," and had already brought them a picture-book. Nastya, the elder, an eight-year-old girl, could read, and Kostya, the boy, seven, loved being read to by her. Krassotkin could, of course, have come up with livelier entertainment for them. He could have lined them up and played soldiers, or sent them off hiding around the house. He'd done that more than once before, and wasn't above doing it again, so much so that a rumor had gone around school that Krassotkin played horses with the little lodgers at home, prancing along with his head cocked to one side like a trace-horse. But Krassotkin haughtily deflected this jab, pointing out that playing horses with boys his own age, boys of thirteen, would certainly be beneath him "at this stage," but that he did it for "the kids'" sake because he liked them, and no one had any right to call him to account over his feelings. The two "kids" adored him.

But this time he was in no mood for games. He had important business of his own ahead of him, something almost mysterious. Meanwhile time was passing, and Agafya, with whom he could have left the children, wouldn't come back from market. He'd already crossed the passage several times, opened the door to the lodgers' room, and looked anxiously in at "the kids," who sat over the book as he'd told them. Every time he opened the door they grinned at him, hoping he'd come in and do something delightful and amusing. But Kolya was preoccupied and didn't go in.

At last it struck eleven, and he made up his mind, once and for all, that if that "cursed" Agafya didn't get back within ten minutes he'd go out without waiting for her, making "the kids" promise, of course, to be brave while he was gone, not to misbehave, not to cry out of fright. With that settled, he put on his padded winter overcoat with its catskin collar, slung his satchel over his shoulder, and — ignoring his mother's constantly repeated pleas that he always wear galoshes in such cold weather — looked at them with contempt as he crossed the hall and went out wearing only his boots. Perezvon, seeing him dressed to go out, began tapping his tail on the floor nervously, but eagerly. Twitching all over, he even let out a plaintive whine. But Kolya, seeing his dog's passionate excitement, decided it was a breach of discipline, kept him under the bench a moment longer, and only whistled for him once he'd opened the door into the passage. The dog sprang up like a wild thing and rushed bounding ahead of him in ecstasy.

Kolya opened the door to look in on "the kids." They were both sitting as before at the table, not reading but arguing hotly about something. The children often argued together about various pressing questions of life, and Nastya, being the elder, usually won. If Kostya didn't agree with her, he almost always appealed to Kolya Krassotkin, and his verdict was treated as infallible by both. This time the "kids'" argument rather interested Krassotkin, and he stood still in the passage to listen. The children saw he was listening, which only made them argue with even greater energy.

"I will never, never believe," Nastya was chattering, "that old women find babies among the cabbages in the vegetable garden. It's winter now, there aren't any cabbages, so the old woman couldn't have brought Katerina a daughter."
Kolya whistled quietly to himself.
"Or maybe they do bring babies from somewhere, but only to people who are married."
Kostya stared at Nastya and listened, pondering it deeply.
"Nastya, how silly you are!" he said finally, firmly and calmly. "How can Katerina have a baby when she isn't married?"
Nastya was exasperated.
"You don't know anything about it," she snapped irritably. "Maybe she has a husband, only he's in prison, so now she's got a baby."
"But is her husband really in prison?" the matter-of-fact Kostya asked gravely.

"Or, I'll tell you what," Nastya interrupted impulsively, entirely dropping and forgetting her first theory. "She doesn't have a husband, you're right about that, but she wants to be married, and so she's been thinking about getting married, and thinking and thinking about it until now she's got it — that is, not a husband, but a baby."
"Well, maybe so," Kostya agreed, thoroughly won over. "But you didn't say that before. So how was I supposed to know?"
"Come, kiddies," said Kolya, stepping into the room. "You're a couple of terrors, I see."
"And Perezvon's with you!" Kostya grinned, and started snapping his fingers and calling Perezvon.

"I'm in a difficulty, kids," Krassotkin began solemnly, "and you have to help me. Agafya must have broken her leg, since she still hasn't shown up — that's certain. I have to go out. Will you let me go?"
The children looked at each other anxiously. Their smiling faces showed a flicker of unease, but they didn't yet fully grasp what was being asked of them.
"You won't be naughty while I'm gone? You won't climb on the cupboard and break your legs? You won't get scared alone and cry?"
A look of deep despondency crossed the children's faces.
"And I could show you something as a reward — a little copper cannon that can be fired with real gunpowder."
The children's faces brightened instantly. "Show us the cannon," said Kostya, beaming all over.
Krassotkin reached into his satchel, pulled out a little bronze cannon, and stood it on the table.
"Ah, of course you'd ask that! Look, it's on wheels." He rolled the toy along the table. "And it can be fired off, too. You can load it with shot and fire it."
"And could it kill someone?"

"It can kill anyone — you just have to aim it at somebody," and Krassotkin explained where the powder went, where the shot rolled in, showing them a tiny hole like a touch-hole, and told them it kicked when it was fired.
The children listened with intense interest. What especially struck their imagination was that the cannon kicked.
"And do you have any powder?" Nastya asked.
"Yes."
"Show us the powder too," she drawled, with a pleading smile.

Krassotkin dove back into his satchel and pulled out a small flask holding a little real gunpowder. He had some shot too, wrapped in a twist of paper. He even uncorked the flask and shook a little powder into his palm.
"You have to be careful there's no fire around, or it would blow up and kill us all," Krassotkin warned them dramatically.
The children stared at the powder with an awestruck alarm that only sharpened their delight. But Kostya liked the shot better.
"And does the shot burn?" he asked.
"No, it doesn't."
"Give me a little shot," he begged.
"I'll give you a little shot — here, take it, but don't show it to your mother until I get back, or she'll be sure to think it's gunpowder, and die of fright, and give you a thrashing."
"Mother never whips us," Nastya remarked at once.

"I know, I just said that to finish the sentence. And don't you ever deceive your mother, except just this once, until I get back. So, kiddies — can I go out? You won't cry and get scared while I'm gone?"
"We sha—all cry," Kostya drawled, already on the verge of tears.
"We shall cry, we're sure to cry," Nastya chimed in, with timid haste.
"Oh, children, children, what a dangerous age you're at! There's no help for it, chicks, I'll have to stay with you, I don't know how long. And time's passing, time's passing, oogh!"
"Tell Perezvon to play dead!" Kostya begged.
"There's no help for it, we'll have to fall back on Perezvon. _Ici_, Perezvon." And Kolya began giving the dog orders, and he ran through all his tricks.

He was a rough-coated dog of medium size, with a sort of lilac-gray coat. He was blind in his right eye, and his left ear was torn. He whined and jumped, stood and walked on his hind legs, lay on his back with his paws in the air, stiff as though dead. While this last trick was going on, the door opened and Agafya, Madame Krassotkin's servant, a stout, pockmarked woman of forty, appeared in the doorway. She'd come back from market with a bag full of provisions in her hand. Holding the bag up in her left hand, she stood still to watch the dog. Though Kolya had been so anxious for her to get back, he didn't cut the performance short, and after keeping Perezvon dead the usual length of time, he finally whistled to him. The dog jumped up and bounded about joyfully at having done his duty.
"Just fancy, a dog!" Agafya observed sententiously.
"Why are you late, woman?" Krassotkin asked sternly.
"Woman, indeed! Go on with you, you brat."
"Brat?"

"Yes, a brat. What's it to you if I'm late? If I'm late, you can be sure I had a good reason," Agafya muttered, busying herself about the stove, without a trace of anger or irritation in her voice. She actually seemed pleased to enjoy a little skirmish with her merry young master.

"Listen, you frivolous woman," Krassotkin began, getting up from the sofa, "can you swear on everything you hold sacred in the world, and something more besides, that you'll keep a close watch on the kids while I'm away? I'm going out."
"And what would I swear for?" laughed Agafya. "I'll watch them without that."
"No, you have to swear on your eternal salvation. Otherwise I won't go."
"Well, then don't. What does it matter to me? It's cold out — stay home."

"Kids," Kolya turned to the children, "this woman will stay with you until I get back, or until your mother comes home, since she really ought to have been back long ago. She'll give you lunch too. You'll feed them, Agafya, won't you?"
"I can do that."

"Goodbye, chickens, I'm going with my mind at ease. And you, granny," he added gravely, in an undertone, as he passed Agafya, "I hope you'll spare their tender years and not tell them any of your old woman's nonsense about Katerina. _Ici_, Perezvon!"
"Get along with you!" Agafya retorted, genuinely angry now. "Ridiculous boy! You need a whipping, talking like that!"

title: III. The Schoolboy
paragraphs: But Kolya didn't hear her. At last he could go out. As he stepped out at the gate he looked around, hunched his shoulders, said "It's freezing," and went straight down the street, turning off to the right toward the market square. When he reached the second-to-last house before the market square, he stopped at the gate, pulled a whistle from his pocket, and blew it with all his might, like a signal. He didn't have to wait more than a minute before a rosy-cheeked boy of about eleven, wearing a warm, neat, even stylish coat, darted out to meet him. This was Smurov, a boy in the preparatory class (two years below Kolya Krassotkin), the son of a well-to-do official. He was apparently forbidden by his parents to associate with Krassotkin, who was well known as a hopelessly naughty boy, so Smurov was clearly slipping out on the sly. He was — if the reader hasn't forgotten — one of the group of boys who, two months before, had thrown stones at Ilusha. He was the one who told Alyosha Karamazov about Ilusha.
"I've been waiting for you for the last hour, Krassotkin," said Smurov flatly, and the boys strode toward the market square.
"I'm late," answered Krassotkin. "I was held up by circumstances. You won't get thrashed for being seen with me?"
"Come on, I'm never thrashed! And you've got Perezvon with you?"
"Yes."
"You're taking him too?"
"Yes."
"Ah! If only it were Zhutchka!"
"Impossible. Zhutchka doesn't exist. Zhutchka is lost in the mists of obscurity."

"Ah! Couldn't we do this?" Smurov suddenly stopped. "You see, Ilusha says Zhutchka was a shaggy, grayish, smoky-looking dog, like Perezvon. Couldn't you tell him this is Zhutchka, and maybe he'd believe you?"
"Boy, shun a lie — that's one thing; even for a good purpose — that's another. Above all, I hope you haven't told anyone that I'm coming."

"Heaven forbid! I know what I'm doing. But you won't comfort him with Perezvon," said Smurov, with a sigh. "You know his father, the captain, the 'wisp of tow,' told us he was going to bring him a real mastiff pup, with a black nose, today. He thinks that would comfort Ilusha, but I doubt it."
"And how is Ilusha?"

"Ah, he's bad, very bad! I think he's got consumption: he's fully conscious, but his breathing's off. It's gone wrong. The other day he asked to have his boots put on so he could be walked around the room. He tried to walk, but couldn't stand. 'Ah, I told you before, father,' he said, 'that those boots were no good. I could never walk properly in them.' He imagined it was his boots making him stagger, but really it was just weakness. He won't live another week. Herzenstube's looking after him. Now they're rich again — they've got heaps of money."
"They're rogues."
"Who's rogues?"

"Doctors, and the whole tribe of quacks, collectively — and individually too, of course. I don't believe in medicine. It's a useless institution. I mean to look into all that someday. But what's this sentimentality you've all got going up there? The whole class seems to be there every day."
"Not the whole class — only about ten of us go to see him every day. There's nothing in that."

"What I don't understand in all this is what part Alexey Karamazov is playing. His brother's going to be tried tomorrow or the day after for a crime like that, and yet he has so much time to spend on sentimentality with schoolboys."
"There's no sentimentality about it. You're going yourself right now to make peace with Ilusha."
"Make peace with him? What an absurd way to put it! But I won't have anyone analyzing my actions."
"And how pleased Ilusha will be to see you! He has no idea you're coming. Why was it, why was it you wouldn't come all this time?" Smurov cried, with sudden warmth.

"My dear boy, that's my business, not yours. I'm going because I choose to; but all of you were hauled there by Alexey Karamazov — there's a difference, you know. And how do you know? Maybe I'm not going to make peace with him at all. It's a stupid expression."

"It's not Karamazov at all — it's not his doing. Our fellows started going there on their own. Of course, at first they went with Karamazov. And there was nothing of that sort about it — no silliness. First one went, then another. His father was terribly pleased to see us. You know he'll simply go out of his mind if Ilusha dies. He can see Ilusha is dying. And he seems so glad we made peace with Ilusha. Ilusha just asked after you, that was all. He just asks, and says nothing more. His father will go out of his mind or hang himself. He acted like a madman before. You know he's a very decent man. We made a mistake back then. It's all the fault of that murderer who beat him."

"Karamazov's a riddle to me, all the same. I could have made his acquaintance long ago, but I like to have a proper pride in some matters. Besides, I have a theory about him I still need to work out and confirm."

Kolya lapsed into dignified silence. Smurov, too, was quiet. Smurov, of course, worshipped Krassotkin and never dreamed of putting himself on his level. Now he was tremendously intrigued by Kolya's saying he was "going of his own accord" to see Ilusha. He sensed there must be some mystery in Kolya's suddenly deciding to go see him that day. They crossed the market square, which at that hour held many loaded wagons in from the country and a great number of live fowls. The market women sold rolls, cottons, threads and so on from their stalls. These Sunday markets were naively called "fairs" in the town, and there were many such fairs through the year.
Perezvon ran about in the highest spirits, sniffing first one way, then the other. When he met other dogs they zealously sniffed each other over, following the rules of canine etiquette.
"I like watching realistic little scenes like that, Smurov," said Kolya suddenly. "Have you noticed how dogs sniff each other when they meet? It seems to be a law of their nature."
"Yes; it's a funny habit."

"No, it's not funny; you're wrong there. There's nothing funny in nature, no matter how funny it may look to man with his prejudices. If dogs could reason and criticize us, they'd be sure to find just as much that struck them as funny — if not more — in the social habits of men, their masters. Far more, in fact. I say that because I'm convinced there's far more foolishness among us. That's Rakitin's idea — a remarkable idea. I'm a Socialist, Smurov."
"And what's a Socialist?" asked Smurov.

"It's when everyone's equal, and all property is held in common, there are no marriages, and everyone can have whatever religion and laws they like best, and all the rest of it. You're not old enough to understand that yet. It's cold, though."
"Yes, twelve degrees of frost. Father just looked at the thermometer."

"Have you noticed, Smurov, that in the middle of winter we don't feel the cold as much, even at fifteen or eighteen degrees of frost, as we do now, at the start of winter, when there's a sudden frost of twelve degrees, especially when there isn't much snow yet? It's because people aren't used to it. Everything is habit with human beings, everything, even in their social and political relations. Habit is the great driving force. What a funny-looking peasant!"

Kolya pointed to a tall peasant with a good-natured face, in a long sheepskin coat, standing by his wagon, clapping his hands together in their shapeless leather gloves to warm them. His long fair beard was white with frost.
"That peasant's beard is frozen," Kolya called out in a loud, provoking voice as he passed him.
"Plenty of people's beards are frozen," the peasant replied, calm and matter-of-fact.
"Don't provoke him," Smurov said.
"It's all right, he won't get cross — he's a nice fellow. Goodbye, Matvey."
"Goodbye."
"Is your name Matvey?"
"Yes. Didn't you know?"
"No, I didn't. It was a guess."
"You don't say! You're a schoolboy, I take it?"
"Yes."
"You get whipped, I expect?"
"Nothing much — sometimes."
"Does it hurt?"
"Well, yes, it does."
"Eh, what a life!" The peasant heaved a sigh from the bottom of his heart.
"Goodbye, Matvey."
"Goodbye. You're a nice lad, that you are."
The boys walked on.
"That was a nice peasant," Kolya remarked to Smurov. "I like talking to peasants, and I'm always glad to give them their due."
"Why did you lie, pretending we get whipped?" asked Smurov.
"I had to say that to please him."
"How do you mean?"

"You know, Smurov, I don't like being asked the same thing twice. I like people to catch on at the first word. Some things can't be explained. In a peasant's view, schoolboys are whipped, and ought to be whipped. What would a schoolboy even be if he weren't whipped? And if I told him we weren't, he'd be disappointed. But you don't understand that. You have to know how to talk to peasants."
"Only don't tease them, please, or you'll get into another scrape like the one with the goose."
"So you're scared?"
"Don't laugh, Kolya. Of course I'm scared. My father would be awfully cross. I'm strictly forbidden to go out with you."
"Don't worry, nothing will happen this time. Hallo, Natasha!" he shouted to a market woman at one of the stalls.
"Call me Natasha! What next! My name's Marya," the middle-aged market woman shouted back.
"I'm glad it's Marya. Goodbye!"
"Ah, you young rascal! A brat like you, carrying on like that!"
"I'm in a hurry. Can't stay now. You can tell me next Sunday." Kolya waved his hand at her, as if she'd attacked him and not the other way around.
"I've nothing to tell you next Sunday. You went after me, you impudent young monkey, I didn't say a thing," Marya bawled. "You need a whipping, that's what you need, you saucy jackanapes!"

There was a roar of laughter among the other market women around her. Suddenly a man in a furious temper darted out from the arcade of shops nearby. He was a young man, not a local, with dark curly hair and a long, pale, pockmarked face. He wore a long blue coat and a peaked cap, and looked like a merchant's clerk. He was in a state of stupid excitement and shook his fist at Kolya.
"I know you!" he cried angrily. "I know you!"
Kolya stared at him. He couldn't recall when he might have had a run-in with the man. But he'd been in so many street scrapes he could hardly remember them all.
"Do you?" he asked sarcastically.
"I know you! I know you!" the man repeated idiotically.
"So much the better for you. Well, it's time I was going. Goodbye!"
"Up to your saucy pranks again, are you?" the man cried. "Up to your saucy pranks again? I know it, you're at it again!"
"It's none of your business, brother, if I'm up to my saucy pranks again," said Kolya, standing still and looking him over.
"Not my business?"
"No; it's not your business."
"Whose, then? Whose, then? Whose, then?"
"It's Trifon Nikititch's business, not yours."
"What Trifon Nikititch?" the youth asked, staring at Kolya with loutish astonishment, still as furious as ever.
Kolya looked him over gravely.
"Have you been to the Church of the Ascension?" he suddenly asked, with stern emphasis.
"What Church of the Ascension? What for? No, I haven't," said the young man, somewhat thrown off.
"Do you know Sabaneyev?" Kolya went on, even more emphatically, even more sternly.
"What Sabaneyev? I don't know him."

"Well then, you can go to the devil," said Kolya, cutting the conversation short, and, turning sharply right, he strode off quickly, as though he disdained to say another word to a blockhead who didn't even know Sabaneyev.
"Stop, hey! What Sabaneyev?" the young man, shaking off his momentary stupor, was as worked up as before. "What did he mean?" He turned to the market women with a blank stare.
The women laughed.
"You never can tell what he's after," one of them said.
"What Sabaneyev is he talking about?" the young man repeated, still furious and waving his right arm.
"Must be a Sabaneyev who worked for the Kuzmitchovs, that's who it must be," one of the women suggested.
The young man stared at her wildly.
"For the Kuzmitchovs?" another woman repeated. "But his name wasn't Trifon. His name's Kuzma, not Trifon; but the boy said Trifon Nikititch, so it can't be the same one."
"His name isn't Trifon and it isn't Sabaneyev, it's Tchizhov," a third woman put in suddenly, who'd been silent until now, listening gravely. "Alexey Ivanitch is his name. Tchizhov, Alexey Ivanitch."
"No doubt about it, it's Tchizhov," a fourth woman confirmed emphatically.
The bewildered youth stared from one to another.
"But what did he ask for, what did he ask for, good people?" he cried, almost in despair. "'Do you know Sabaneyev?' he says. And who the devil's supposed to know who Sabaneyev is?"
"You're a hopeless fellow. I'm telling you it's not Sabaneyev, it's Tchizhov, Alexey Ivanitch Tchizhov, that's who it is!" one of the women shouted at him, impressed with herself.
"What Tchizhov? Who is he? Tell me, if you know."
"That tall, sniveling fellow who used to sit in the market in the summer."
"And what's your Tchizhov to do with me, good people, eh?"

"How should I know what he's got to do with you?" put in another. "You ought to know that yourself, if you're making such a fuss about him. He spoke to you, not to us, you fool. Don't you really know him?"
"Know who?"
"Tchizhov."
"The devil take Tchizhov, and you along with him. I'll give him a hiding, that I will. He was laughing at me!"
"Give Tchizhov a hiding! More likely he'll give you one. You're a fool, that's what you are!"
"Not Tchizhov, not Tchizhov, you spiteful, mischief-making woman. I'll give the boy a hiding. Catch him, catch him, he was laughing at me!"

The woman burst out laughing. But by now Kolya was a long way off, marching along with a triumphant air. Smurov walked beside him, glancing back at the shouting group behind them. He too was in high spirits, though still a little afraid of landing in some scrape with Kolya.
"What Sabaneyev did you mean?" he asked Kolya, already guessing what the answer would be.

"How should I know? Now there'll be an uproar among them all day long. I like stirring up fools in every walk of life. There's another blockhead — that peasant over there. You know how they say 'there's no one stupider than a stupid Frenchman,' but a stupid Russian shows it right on his face too. Can't you see it all over that peasant's face that he's a fool, eh?"
"Leave him alone, Kolya. Let's go on."
"Nothing's going to stop me now that I'm started. Hey there, good morning, peasant!"
A sturdy-looking peasant with a round, simple face and a grizzled beard, walking by, raised his head and looked at the boy. He seemed not quite sober.
"Good morning, if you're not laughing at me," he said deliberately.
"And if I am?" Kolya laughed.
"Well, a joke's a joke. Laugh away, I don't mind. There's no harm in a joke."
"I beg your pardon, brother, it was a joke."
"Well, God forgive you!"
"Do you forgive me too?"
"I forgive you entirely. Go along."
"I say, you seem a clever peasant."
"Cleverer than you," the peasant answered unexpectedly, with the same gravity.
"I doubt it," said Kolya, somewhat thrown off.
"It's true, though."
"Perhaps it is."
"It is, brother."
"Goodbye, peasant!"
"Goodbye!"
"There are all sorts of peasants," Kolya remarked to Smurov after a brief silence. "How was I supposed to know I'd run into a clever one? I'm always ready to recognize intelligence in a peasant."

In the distance the cathedral clock struck half past eleven. The boys hurried, and walked the considerable distance to Captain Snegiryov's lodgings quickly and almost in silence. Twenty paces from the house Kolya stopped and told Smurov to go on ahead and ask Karamazov to come out to him.
"One has to sniff around a bit first," he remarked to Smurov.
"Why ask him to come outside?" Smurov protested. "Just go in, they'll be delighted to see you. What's the point of making friends out here in the frost?"
"I know why I want to see him out here in the frost," Kolya cut him off, in the imperious tone he liked to take with "small boys," and Smurov ran off to do as he was told.

title: IV. The Lost Dog
paragraphs: Kolya leaned against the fence with an air of dignity, waiting for Alyosha to appear. Yes, he'd long wanted to meet him. He'd heard a great deal about him from the other boys, but until now he'd always kept up an air of disdainful indifference whenever Alyosha was mentioned, and had even "criticized" what he'd heard about him. But secretly he was dying to make his acquaintance; there was something appealing and attractive in everything he'd been told about Alyosha. So this moment mattered: first of all, he had to show himself at his best, to show his independence. "Or he'll take me for thirteen and treat me like the rest of them. And what are these boys to him anyway? I'll ask him once I know him. It's a pity I'm so short, though. Tuzikov's younger than me, and yet he's half a head taller. But I have a clever face. I'm not good-looking, I know I'm ugly, but I have a clever face. I mustn't talk too freely — if I throw myself at him all at once, he might think — ugh! how awful if he thought—!"

Such were the thoughts racing through Kolya's mind while he did his utmost to look as independent as possible. What distressed him most wasn't so much his "ugly" face as his being so short. On the wall in a corner at home he'd made a pencil mark the year before to record his height, and every two months since then he'd anxiously measured himself against it to see how much he'd grown. But alas, he grew very slowly, and this sometimes drove him nearly to despair. His face, in fact, was by no means "ugly"; on the contrary, it was rather appealing — fair, pale skin, freckled. His small, lively gray eyes had a fearless look and often lit up with feeling. He had rather high cheekbones, small, very red, but not very full lips; his nose was small and unmistakably turned up. "I've got a real pug nose, a real pug nose," Kolya used to mutter to himself when he looked in the mirror, and always walked away indignant. "But maybe I don't even have a clever face?" he'd sometimes think, doubtful even of that. But it shouldn't be assumed his mind dwelled on his face and height. On the contrary, however bitter those moments before the mirror, he forgot them quickly, and for a long time, "giving himself over entirely to ideas and to real life," as he put it to himself.

Alyosha came out quickly and hurried up to Kolya. Before he even reached him, Kolya could see he looked delighted. "Can he really be that glad to see me?" Kolya wondered, pleased. We might note here, in passing, that Alyosha's appearance had completely changed since we last saw him. He'd given up the cassock and now wore a well-cut coat, a soft round hat, and had his hair cropped short. All of it suited him very well, and he looked quite handsome. His charming face always had a good-humored look; but there was gentleness and calm in his good humor. To Kolya's surprise, Alyosha came out to him just as he was, without an overcoat — clearly he'd hurried out. He held out his hand to Kolya at once.
"Here you are at last! How anxiously we've been waiting for you!"

"There were reasons, which you'll learn shortly. Anyway, I'm glad to make your acquaintance. I've been hoping for the chance a long time, and have heard a great deal about you," Kolya muttered, a little breathless.
"We'd have met anyway. I've heard a great deal about you too — but you've taken a long time getting here."
"Tell me, how are things?"
"Ilusha is very ill. He's certainly dying."
"How awful! You must admit medicine is a fraud, Karamazov," Kolya cried warmly.

"Ilusha has mentioned you often, very often, even in his sleep, in his delirium, you know. One can see you used to mean a great deal to him ... before the incident ... with the knife.... There's another reason too.... Tell me, is that your dog?"
"Yes, Perezvon."
"Not Zhutchka?" Alyosha looked at Kolya with eyes full of pity. "Is she lost for good?"

"I know you'd all like it to be Zhutchka. I've heard all about it." Kolya smiled mysteriously. "Listen, Karamazov, I'll tell you the whole thing. That's what I came for — that's why I asked you to come out here, to explain the whole episode before we go in," he began animatedly. "You see, Karamazov, Ilusha came into the preparatory class last spring. Well, you know what our preparatory class is like — a pack of little boys. They started teasing Ilusha right away. I'm two classes above, so of course I only watch from a distance. I saw the boy was weak and small, but he wouldn't give in to them; he fought back. I saw he was proud, and his eyes were full of fire. I like children like that. And they only teased him more for it. Worst of all, he was dressed horribly at the time — his trousers were too small for him, and his boots had holes in them. They gave him grief over it, jeered at him. That I can't stand. I stood up for him right away and gave it to them hot. I beat them, but they adore me, you know, Karamazov?" Kolya boasted impulsively. "But I've always had a soft spot for children. I've got two chicks at home in my hands right now — that's what kept me today. So they left off beating Ilusha, and I took him under my wing. I saw the boy was proud, I tell you, the boy was proud — but in the end he became devoted to me like a slave: did my every bidding, obeyed me as if I were God, tried to copy me. Between classes he'd run straight to me, and I'd go around with him. Sundays too. People always laugh when an older boy makes friends with a younger one like that, but that's just prejudice. If it's my own choice, that's enough. I'm teaching him, developing him. Why shouldn't I develop him if I like him? You, Karamazov, have taken up with all these fledglings yourself. I can see you want to influence the younger generation — to develop them, to be useful to them — and I assure you, this trait of your character, which I knew about by hearsay, drew me to you more than anything. But let's get to the point. I noticed a kind of softness, a sentimentality, creeping over the boy, and you know I have an absolute hatred of this soppy sentimentality, I've had it since I was a baby. There were contradictions in him too: he was proud, yet slavishly devoted to me, and then suddenly his eyes would flash and he'd refuse to agree with me, argue, fly into a rage. I'd sometimes put forward certain ideas; I could see it wasn't so much that he disagreed with the ideas as that he was simply rebelling against me, because I was cool in the face of his affection. So, in order to train him properly, the tenderer he got, the colder I became. I did it on purpose — that was my plan. My goal was to shape his character, to lick him into form, to make a man of him ... and besides ... no doubt you follow me without my spelling it out. Suddenly I noticed that for three days running he was gloomy and downcast, not because of my coldness, but over something else, something more serious. I wondered what the trouble was. I pressed him and found out he'd somehow gotten to know Smerdyakov, who was footman to your late father — this was before his death, of course — and Smerdyakov had taught the poor fool a stupid trick, that is, a brutal, nasty trick. He told him to take a piece of bread, stick a pin in it, and throw it to one of those hungry dogs that snap up anything without chewing it, and then watch what happened. So they prepared a piece of bread like that and threw it to Zhutchka, that shaggy dog there's been all this fuss about. The people who owned it never fed it at all, though it barked all day. (Do you like that stupid barking, Karamazov? I can't stand it.) So it lunged at the bread, swallowed it, and started to squeal — it turned round and round and ran off, squealing as it went, out of sight. That was Ilusha's own account of it. He confessed it to me, crying bitterly. He hugged me, shaking all over. He kept repeating, 'He ran off squealing' — the sight of it haunted him. I could see he was tormented by remorse. I took it seriously. I decided to teach him a lesson about other things too, while I was at it. So I'll admit I wasn't entirely straight with him — I pretended to be more outraged than I really was. 'You've done a rotten thing,' I said, 'you're a scoundrel. I won't tell on you, of course, but I'll have nothing more to do with you for a while. I'll think it over and let you know through Smurov' — that's the boy who just came with me, he's always ready to do anything for me — 'whether I'll have anything more to do with you in the future, or whether I write you off for good as a scoundrel.' He was tremendously upset. I'll admit I felt I'd gone too far as I was saying it, but there was no helping it — I did what I thought was right at the time. A day or two later, I sent Smurov to tell him I wouldn't speak to him again. That's what we call it when two schoolfellows cut each other off entirely. Privately, I only meant to send him to Coventry for a few days, and then, if I saw signs of repentance, hold out my hand to him again. That was my plan. But do you know what happened? He heard Smurov's message, and his eyes flashed. 'Tell Krassotkin from me,' he cried, 'that I'll throw bread with pins in it to every dog there is — every last one!'
