'So he's got a bit of a temper on him. We'll have to smoke that out of him.' And I started treating him with contempt; whenever I ran into him I'd turn away or smile sarcastically. And right about then, that business with his father happened. You remember? You have to understand he was already worked up to a fever pitch over what had already happened. The boys, seeing I'd given him up, went after him and taunted him, shouting, 'Wisp of tow, wisp of tow!' And soon there were regular skirmishes with them, which I'm very sorry about now. They seem to have given him one particularly bad beating. One day he flew at all of them as they came out of school. I was standing a few yards off, watching. And I swear, I don't remember laughing — quite the opposite, I felt terribly sorry for him, and in another minute I'd have run over to take his side. But he suddenly met my eyes. I don't know what he imagined, but he pulled out a penknife, rushed at me, and struck at my thigh, here, in my right leg. I didn't move. I don't mind admitting I have my nerve sometimes, Karamazov. I simply looked at him with contempt, as if to say, 'This is how you repay all my kindness! Do it again if you like, I'm at your service.' But he didn't stab me again; he broke down, terrified of what he'd done, threw away the knife, burst into tears, and ran off. I didn't rat on him, of course, and I made everyone keep quiet, so it wouldn't reach the masters. I didn't even tell my mother until it had healed. And the wound was barely a scratch. And then I heard that the same day he'd been throwing stones and had bitten your finger — but you understand now what state he was in! Well, it can't be helped: it was stupid of me not to come and forgive him — that is, make peace with him — once he fell ill. I regret it now. But I had a particular reason. So now I've told you the whole thing ... though I'm afraid it was stupid of me."

"Oh, what a shame," Alyosha exclaimed, with feeling, "that I didn't know before what things stood between you two, or I'd have come to you long ago to beg you to come with me to see him. Would you believe it, when he was feverish he talked about you in his delirium. I had no idea how much you meant to him! And you really haven't managed to find that dog? His father and the boys have been hunting all over town for it. Would you believe it, since he's been ill I've heard him say, three times, with tears, 'It's because I killed Zhutchka, father, that I'm sick now. God is punishing me for it.' He can't get the idea out of his head. And if the dog were found and turned out to be alive, one might almost imagine the joy of it would cure him. We've all pinned our hopes on you."
"Tell me, what made you hope I'd be the one to find him?" Kolya asked, intensely curious. "Why did you count on me rather than anyone else?"

"There was a rumor going around that you were looking for the dog, and that you'd bring it once you found it. Smurov said something of the sort. We've all been trying to convince Ilusha the dog is alive, that it's been seen. The boys brought him a live hare; he just looked at it with a faint smile and asked them to let it go in the fields. So we did. His father just this minute got back, bringing him a mastiff pup, hoping to comfort him with that — but I think it only makes things worse."
"Tell me, Karamazov, what sort of man is the father? I know him, but what do you make of him — a mountebank, a buffoon?"

"Oh, no; there are people of deep feeling who've somehow been crushed. Buffoonery in people like that is a kind of resentful irony against those they don't dare tell the truth to, from years of being humiliated and intimidated by them. Believe me, Krassotkin, that sort of buffoonery is sometimes tragic in the extreme. His whole life now centers on Ilusha, and if Ilusha dies, he'll either go mad with grief or kill himself. I feel almost certain of that when I look at him now."
"I understand you, Karamazov. I can see you understand human nature," Kolya added, with feeling.
"And the moment I saw you with a dog, I thought you were bringing Zhutchka."

"Wait a bit, Karamazov, maybe we'll still find him yet; but this is Perezvon. I'll let him in now, and maybe it'll cheer Ilusha up more than the mastiff pup did. Wait a bit, Karamazov, you'll see something in a minute. But, I say, I'm keeping you standing here!" Kolya cried suddenly. "You've got no overcoat on in this bitter cold. You see what an egoist I am. Oh, we're all egoists, Karamazov!"
"Don't worry about it — it's cold, but I don't catch cold easily. Let's go in, though, and, by the way, what's your name? I know you're called Kolya, but what else?"
"Nikolay — Nikolay Ivanovitch Krassotkin, or, as they say in official documents, 'son of Krassotkin.'" Kolya laughed for some reason, but then added suddenly, "Of course I hate my name, Nikolay."
"Why is that?"
"It's so trivial, so ordinary."
"You're thirteen?" Alyosha asked.

"No, fourteen — that is, I'll be fourteen very soon, in a fortnight. I'll confess one weakness of mine to you, Karamazov, just to you, since this is our first meeting, so you can understand my character right away. I hate being asked my age — more than that ... and actually ... there's a slanderous story going around about me, that last week I was playing robbers with the preparatory boys. It's true I played with them, but it's a complete slander to say I did it for my own amusement. I have reason to believe you've heard the story; but I wasn't playing for my own amusement, it was for the children's sake, because they couldn't think up anything to do on their own. But they always have some silly tale going around. This is an awful town for gossip, I can tell you."
"But what if you had been playing for your own amusement — what's the harm in that?"
"Come now, my own amusement! You don't play horses, do you?"

"But you have to look at it this way," Alyosha said, smiling. "Grown-ups go to the theater, and there the adventures of all sorts of heroes are acted out — sometimes there are robbers and battles too — and isn't that just the same thing, in a different form, of course? And young people's games of soldiers or robbers in their free time are also art in its earliest stage. You know, they spring from the same growing artistic instincts in the young. And sometimes these games are much better than performances at the theater — the only difference is that people go there to watch actors, while in these games the young people are the actors themselves. But that's only natural."

"You think so? Is that your idea?" Kolya looked at him intently. "Oh, you know, that's actually a rather interesting way of looking at it. When I get home, I'll think it over. I'll admit I thought I might learn something from you. I've come to learn from you, Karamazov," Kolya concluded, in a voice full of unguarded feeling.
"And I from you," said Alyosha, smiling and pressing his hand.
Kolya was very pleased with Alyosha. What struck him most was that Alyosha treated him exactly as an equal, talking to him just as though he were "fully grown up."
"I'll show you something in a minute, Karamazov — it's a bit of theater, too," he said, laughing nervously. "That's why I came."
"Let's go first to the landlord's, on the left. All the boys leave their coats there, since the room's small and hot."

"Oh, I'm only coming in for a minute. I'll keep my overcoat on. Perezvon will stay here in the hallway and play dead. _Ici_, Perezvon, lie down and be dead! You see how dead he is. I'll go in first and scout around, then I'll whistle for him when I think it's time, and you'll see, he'll dash in like mad. Only Smurov mustn't forget to open the door at the right moment. I'll arrange it all — you'll see something."

title: V. By Ilusha’s Bedside
paragraphs: The room occupied by the family of the retired captain Snegiryov is already familiar to the reader. It was close and crowded just then with a number of visitors. Several boys were sitting with Ilusha, and though all of them, like Smurov, would have denied that it was Alyosha who'd brought them there and reconciled them with Ilusha, that was in fact the truth. All the skill he'd used had been to bring them, one by one, to see Ilusha, without any "soppy sentimentality," making it look casual and unplanned. It was a great comfort to Ilusha in his suffering. He was deeply touched by the almost tender affection and sympathy these boys — his former enemies — showed him. Krassotkin was the only one missing, and his absence weighed heavily on Ilusha's heart. Perhaps the bitterest of all his bitter memories was stabbing Krassotkin, who had been his one friend and protector. Clever little Smurov, the first to make peace with Ilusha, thought that was the reason. But when Smurov hinted to Krassotkin that Alyosha wanted to come see him about something, Krassotkin cut him off, telling Smurov to tell "Karamazov" right away that he knew perfectly well what to do, that he wanted no one's advice, and that if he went to see Ilusha he'd choose his own time, since he had "his own reasons."

That was a fortnight before this Sunday. That was why Alyosha hadn't gone to see him, as he'd meant to. But though he waited, he sent Smurov to him twice more. Both times Krassotkin met him with a curt, impatient refusal, sending word back to Alyosha not to bother him anymore, and that if he came himself, he, Krassotkin, wouldn't go to Ilusha's at all. Right up until the last day, Smurov had no idea Kolya meant to go to Ilusha's that morning, and only the evening before, as he parted from Smurov, Kolya abruptly told him to wait at home for him the next morning, since he'd go with him to the Snegiryovs' — but warned him not to breathe a word that he was coming, since he wanted to drop in casually. Smurov obeyed. Smurov's guess that Kolya would bring back the lost dog was based on something Kolya had let slip — that "they must be asses not to find the dog, if it's alive." When Smurov, waiting for the right moment, timidly hinted at his guess about the dog, Krassotkin flew into a violent rage. "I'm not such an ass as to go hunting all over town for other people's dogs when I've got a dog of my own! And how can you imagine a dog could stay alive after swallowing a pin? Soppy sentimentality, that's all it is!"

For the last fortnight Ilusha hadn't left his little bed under the icons in the corner. He hadn't been to school since the day he met Alyosha and bit his finger. He fell ill that very same day, though for a month afterward he could sometimes still get up and walk around the room and hallway. But lately he'd grown so weak he couldn't move without his father's help. His father was terribly worried about him. He'd even given up drinking and was nearly out of his mind with fear that his boy would die. And often, especially after leading him around the room on his arm and putting him back to bed, he'd rush off to a dark corner in the hallway, lean his head against the wall, and break into fits of violent weeping, stifling his sobs so Ilusha wouldn't hear them.

Coming back into the room, he'd usually start doing something to amuse and comfort his precious boy — telling him stories, funny anecdotes, or mimicking comic people he'd happened to meet, even imitating the howls and cries of animals. But Ilusha couldn't bear watching his father clown and play the buffoon. Though the boy tried not to show how much he disliked it, he saw, with an aching heart, that his father was an object of ridicule, and he was continually haunted by the memory of the "wisp of tow" and that "terrible day."

Nina, Ilusha's gentle, crippled sister, didn't care for her father's buffoonery either (Varvara had gone off some time before to Petersburg to study at the university). But the half-witted mother found it hugely entertaining, and laughed heartily whenever her husband started capering about or performing something. It was the only way she could be amused; the rest of the time she grumbled and complained that everyone had forgotten her now, that no one treated her with respect, that she was slighted, and so on. But over the last few days she'd changed completely. She'd started staring constantly at Ilusha's bed in the corner, seeming lost in thought. She was quieter, more subdued, and, if she cried, she cried softly so as not to be heard. The captain noticed the change in her with mournful bewilderment. The boys' visits had at first only irritated her, but later their cheerful shouting and stories began to entertain her, and eventually she grew so fond of them that, if the boys had stopped coming, she'd have felt lonely without them. When the children told a story or played a game, she laughed and clapped her hands. She called some of them over and kissed them. She was especially fond of Smurov.

As for the captain, having the children in his room, coming to cheer up Ilusha, filled his heart from the start with ecstatic joy. He even hoped Ilusha would now shake off his depression, and that it would speed his recovery. Despite his fear for Ilusha, he hadn't, until lately, doubted for a moment that his boy would ultimately recover.

He greeted his young visitors with deference, waited on them hand and foot, and was ready to be their horse — even let them ride on his back — but Ilusha didn't like the game, so it was dropped. He started buying little treats for them, gingerbread and nuts, gave them tea, cut them sandwiches. It should be noted that all this time he had plenty of money. He'd taken the two hundred roubles from Katerina Ivanovna, just as Alyosha had predicted he would. And afterward Katerina Ivanovna, learning more about their circumstances and about Ilusha's illness, visited them herself, got to know the family, and managed to charm the half-witted mother. Since then she'd been generous in helping them, and the captain, terrified at the thought his boy might be dying, set aside his pride and humbly accepted her help.

All this time Doctor Herzenstube, called in by Katerina Ivanovna, came punctually every other day, but little came of his visits, and he dosed the poor invalid mercilessly. But that Sunday morning a new doctor was expected, one who'd come from Moscow with a great reputation. Katerina Ivanovna had sent for him from Moscow at considerable expense, not specifically for Ilusha, but for another purpose, of which more will be said in its place further on. But, since he'd come, she'd asked him to see Ilusha as well, and the captain had been told to expect him. He had no idea whatsoever that Kolya Krassotkin was coming, though he'd long hoped for a visit from the boy Ilusha was pining for.

At the moment Krassotkin opened the door and came into the room, the captain and all the boys were gathered around Ilusha's bed, looking at a tiny mastiff pup, only born the day before, though the captain had ordered it a week earlier to comfort and amuse Ilusha, still grieving over the lost and probably dead Zhutchka. Ilusha, who'd heard three days before that he was to be given a puppy — not just any puppy, but a pedigree mastiff, a very important point, of course — tried, out of delicacy, to pretend he was pleased. But his father and the boys couldn't help seeing that the puppy only served to remind his little heart of the poor dog he'd killed. The puppy lay beside him, feebly stirring, and he, smiling sadly, stroked it with his thin, pale, wasted hand. He clearly liked the puppy, but ... it wasn't Zhutchka; if he could have had both Zhutchka and the puppy, then he'd have been completely happy.
"Krassotkin!" one of the boys suddenly cried. He was the first to see him come in.
Krassotkin's entrance caused a general stir; the boys stepped back and lined up on either side of the bed, so he could see Ilusha clearly. The captain rushed eagerly to meet Kolya.
"Please, come in ... you're most welcome!" he said hurriedly. "Ilusha, Mr. Krassotkin has come to see you!"

But Krassotkin, shaking his hand hastily, immediately demonstrated his complete grasp of proper manners. He turned first to the captain's wife, sitting in her armchair, who was in a rather sour mood just then, grumbling that the boys were standing between her and Ilusha's bed and blocking her view of the new puppy. With the greatest courtesy he bowed to her, scraping his foot, and, turning to Nina, gave her, as the only other lady present, a similar bow. This polite behavior made an extremely favorable impression on the deranged lady.
"There, you can tell at once he's a young man who's been well brought up," she remarked aloud, throwing up her hands; "but as for our other visitors, they come piling in one on top of another."
"What do you mean, mamma, one on top of another? How's that?" the captain muttered affectionately, though with a hint of anxiety on her account.
"That's how they come riding in. They climb on each other's shoulders out in the passage and go prancing in like that, into a respectable family's home. Strange sort of visitors!"
"But who came in like that, mamma?"
"Why, that boy came riding in on that one's back, and this one on that one's."

Kolya was already at Ilusha's bedside. The sick boy went visibly pale. He raised himself in the bed and stared intently at Kolya. Kolya hadn't seen his little friend in two months, and he was stunned at the sight of him. He'd never imagined he'd see such a wasted, yellow face, such huge, feverishly glowing eyes, such thin little hands. He saw, with grieved surprise, Ilusha's quick, labored breathing and his dry lips. He stepped close, held out his hand, and, nearly overcome, said:

"Well, old man ... how are you?" But his voice failed him; he couldn't manage an easy tone; his face suddenly twitched and the corners of his mouth trembled. Ilusha smiled a pitiful little smile, still unable to say a word. Something made Kolya raise his hand and run it over Ilusha's hair.
"Never mind!" he murmured softly, to cheer him up, or maybe without even knowing why he said it. For a minute they were silent again.
"Hey, so you've got a new puppy?" Kolya said suddenly, in a thoroughly offhand voice.
"Ye—es," Ilusha answered in a long whisper, gasping for breath.

"A black nose — that means he'll be fierce, a good watchdog," Kolya observed gravely and stolidly, as though the puppy and its black nose were the only thing on his mind. But in truth he was still struggling with all his might not to burst into tears like a child, and try as he might, he couldn't quite manage it. "When he's grown, you'll have to keep him on a chain, I'm sure."
"He'll be a huge dog!" one of the boys cried.
"Of course he will," "a mastiff," "big," "like this," "big as a calf," several voices shouted.

"Big as a calf, a real calf," the captain chimed in. "I got one like that on purpose, one of the fiercest breeds, and his parents are huge and very fierce — they stand this high off the floor.... Sit down here, on Ilusha's bed, or here on the bench. You're welcome, we've been hoping to see you a long time.... You were kind enough to come with Alexey Fyodorovitch?"
Krassotkin sat on the edge of the bed, at Ilusha's feet. Though he'd perhaps prepared some easy, casual opening for the conversation on the way over, he now completely lost the thread of it.

"No ... I came with Perezvon. I've got a dog now, called Perezvon. A Slavonic name. He's out there ... if I whistle, he'll come running in. I brought a dog too," he said, suddenly addressing Ilusha. "Do you remember Zhutchka, old man?" he fired the question at him abruptly.

Ilusha's little face quivered. He looked at Kolya with an anguished expression. Alyosha, standing by the door, frowned and signaled to Kolya not to mention Zhutchka, but Kolya either didn't notice or wouldn't.
"Where ... is Zhutchka?" Ilusha asked in a broken voice.
"Oh, well, my boy, your Zhutchka's lost and gone for good!"
Ilusha said nothing, but fixed an intent gaze on Kolya once more. Alyosha, catching Kolya's eye, signaled to him again, more urgently, but Kolya looked away, pretending not to notice.

"He must have run off and died somewhere. Must have died after a meal like that," Kolya pronounced pitilessly, though he seemed a little out of breath himself. "But I've got a dog, Perezvon ... a Slavonic name.... I brought him to show you."
"I don't want him!" Ilusha said suddenly.

"No, no, you really must see him ... it'll cheer you up. I brought him on purpose.... He's the same kind of shaggy dog.... Will you let me call my dog in, madam?" he suddenly asked Madame Snegiryov, with an inexplicable excitement in his manner.
"I don't want him, I don't want him!" Ilusha cried, a mournful break in his voice. There was a reproachful light in his eyes.

"You'd better," the captain started up from the chest by the wall, where he'd just sat down, "you'd better ... another time," he muttered, but Kolya couldn't be held back. He hurriedly shouted to Smurov, "Open the door," and as soon as it opened, he blew his whistle. Perezvon dashed headlong into the room.

"Jump, Perezvon, beg! Beg!" Kolya shouted, jumping up, and the dog rose on its hind legs at Ilusha's bedside. What followed took everyone by surprise: Ilusha started, lurched violently forward, bent over Perezvon, and stared at him, faint with suspense.
"It's ... Zhutchka!" he suddenly cried, in a voice breaking with joy and anguish.
"And who did you think it was?" Krassotkin shouted with all his might, in a ringing, joyful voice, and, bending down, he seized the dog and lifted him up to Ilusha.

"Look, old man, you see — blind in one eye, left ear torn, exactly the marks you described to me. That's how I found him. I found him right away. He didn't belong to anyone!" he explained, turning quickly to the captain, to his wife, to Alyosha, and then back to Ilusha. "He'd been living in the Fedotovs' back yard. He made his home there, but they never fed him. He was a stray that had run off from the village ... I found him.... You see, old man, he couldn't have swallowed what you gave him. If he had, he'd have died, he'd have had to! So he must have spat it out, since he's alive. You didn't see him do it. But the pin pricked his tongue, that's why he squealed. He ran off squealing and you thought he'd swallowed it. He might well squeal — the skin inside a dog's mouth is so tender ... much more tender than in people!" Kolya cried impetuously, his face glowing, radiant with delight. Ilusha couldn't speak. White as a sheet, he stared open-mouthed at Kolya, his huge eyes almost starting out of his head. And if Krassotkin, who had no idea of it, had known what a devastating, even fatal effect a moment like this might have on the sick boy's health, nothing would have induced him to play such a trick on him. But Alyosha was perhaps the only person in the room who understood that. As for the captain, he behaved like a small child.
"Zhutchka! It's Zhutchka!" he cried in a voice full of bliss. "Ilusha, this is Zhutchka, your Zhutchka! Mamma, this is Zhutchka!" He was nearly weeping.
"And I never guessed!" Smurov cried regretfully. "Bravo, Krassotkin! I said he'd find the dog, and here he's found him."
"Here he's found him!" another boy echoed gleefully.
"Krassotkin's a brick!" a third voice cried.
"He's a brick, he's a brick!" the other boys cried, and started clapping.

"Wait, wait," Krassotkin did his utmost to shout over them all. "I'll tell you how it happened, that's the whole point. I found him, took him home, and hid him right away. I kept him locked up at home and didn't show him to anyone until today. Only Smurov's known for the last fortnight, but I told him this dog was called Perezvon, and he never guessed. And meanwhile I taught the dog all sorts of tricks. You should see everything he can do! I trained him so I could bring you a well-trained dog, in good condition, old man, so I could say to you, 'See, old man, what a fine dog your Zhutchka is now!' Have you got a bit of meat? He'll show you a trick that'll make you die laughing. A bit of meat, have you got any?"

The captain dashed across the passage to the landlady's, where their cooking was done. Not wanting to lose precious time, Kolya, in desperate haste, shouted to Perezvon, "Dead!" And the dog immediately turned around and lay on his back with all four paws in the air. The boys laughed. Ilusha watched with the same suffering smile, but the one most delighted by the dog's performance was "mamma." She laughed at the dog and began snapping her fingers and calling him, "Perezvon, Perezvon!"

"Nothing will make him get up, nothing!" Kolya cried triumphantly, proud of his success. "He won't budge for all the shouting in the world, but if I call him, he'll jump up in a second. Ici, Perezvon!" The dog leapt up and bounded about, whining with delight. The captain ran back with a piece of cooked beef.

"Is it hot?" Kolya asked briskly, businesslike, taking the meat. "Dogs don't like hot things. No, it's fine. Look, everyone, look, Ilusha, look, old man — why aren't you looking? He's not looking, now that I've brought him."

The new trick was to make the dog stand motionless, nose out, with a tempting bit of meat balanced right on his nose. The luckless dog had to stand without moving, meat balanced on his nose, for as long as his master chose to keep him there — sometimes as long as half an hour. But this time he kept Perezvon waiting only a moment.
"Paid for!" Kolya cried, and the meat flashed from the dog's nose straight into his mouth. The audience, of course, burst into applause and exclamations of amazement.
"Can you really have put off coming all this time simply to train the dog?" Alyosha exclaimed, an unintended note of reproach in his voice.
"Simply for that!" Kolya answered, with perfect simplicity. "I wanted to show him off in all his glory."
"Perezvon! Perezvon," Ilusha called suddenly, snapping his thin fingers and beckoning to the dog.

"What is it? Let him jump up on the bed! _Ici_, Perezvon!" Kolya slapped the bed, and Perezvon sprang up beside Ilusha. The boy threw both arms around his head, and Perezvon instantly licked his cheek. Ilusha pressed close to him, stretched out in bed, and hid his face in the dog's shaggy coat.
"Dear, dear!" the captain kept exclaiming. Kolya sat back down on the edge of the bed.
"Ilusha, I can show you another trick. I've brought you a little cannon. Remember, I told you about it before, and you said how much you'd like to see it. Well, here, I brought it for you."

And Kolya hurriedly pulled the little bronze cannon out of his satchel. He hurried because he was happy himself. Another time he'd have waited for the excitement over Perezvon to die down first, but now he pressed ahead, heedless of any such consideration. "You're all happy now," he felt, "so here's something to make you happier still!" He was utterly delighted himself.

"I've been coveting this thing for a long while — it's for you, old man, it's for you. It belonged to Morozov, it was no use to him, he had it from his brother. I traded him a book from father's bookcase for it — _A Kinsman of Mahomet, or Salutary Folly_, a scandalous book published in Moscow a hundred years ago, before there was any censorship. And Morozov has a taste for that sort of thing. He was grateful to me for it, too...."

Kolya held the cannon in his hand so everyone could see and admire it. Ilusha raised himself, and, still with his right arm around the dog, gazed at the toy in delight. The excitement grew even greater when Kolya announced he had gunpowder too, and that it could be fired off right there "if it won't alarm the ladies." "Mamma" immediately asked to look at the toy up close, and her request was granted. She was thoroughly pleased with the little bronze cannon on wheels, and began rolling it back and forth on her lap. She readily gave permission for the cannon to be fired, without the slightest idea what she was agreeing to. Kolya showed the powder and the shot. The captain, being a military man, took charge of loading it, putting in a tiny amount of powder. He asked that the shot be saved for another time. The cannon was set on the floor, aimed at an empty part of the room, three grains of powder were pushed into the touch-hole, and a match was struck. A magnificent bang followed. Mamma was startled, but immediately laughed with delight. The boys stared in speechless triumph. But the captain, watching Ilusha, was more delighted than any of them. Kolya picked up the cannon and at once presented it to Ilusha, along with the powder and shot.
"I got it for you, for you! I've been saving it for you a long time," he repeated once more, delighted.
"Oh, give it to me! No, give me the cannon!" mamma began begging like a little child. Her face showed a pitiful fear that she wouldn't get it. Kolya was thrown off. The captain fidgeted uneasily.

"Mamma, mamma," he ran to her, "the cannon's yours, of course, but let Ilusha have it, since it's a present to him — but it's just as much yours. Ilusha will always let you play with it; it'll belong to both of you, both of you."
"No, I don't want it to belong to both of us, I want it to be mine, entirely, not Ilusha's," mamma insisted, on the point of tears.

"Take it, mother, here, keep it!" Ilusha cried. "Krassotkin, may I give it to my mother?" he turned to Krassotkin with a pleading face, as though afraid he might be offended at his giving the present away to someone else.
"Of course you may," Krassotkin agreed warmly, and, taking the cannon from Ilusha, handed it himself to mamma with a polite bow. She was so touched she burst into tears.
"Ilusha, darling, he's the one who loves his mamma!" she said tenderly, and immediately began wheeling the cannon back and forth on her lap again.
"Mamma, let me kiss your hand." The captain darted up to her at once and did so.
"And I've never seen such a charming fellow as this nice boy," said the grateful lady, pointing at Krassotkin.

"And I'll bring you as much powder as you like, Ilusha. We make our own powder now. Borovikov figured out how it's done — twenty-four parts saltpeter, ten of sulphur, and six of birchwood charcoal. It's all ground together, mixed into a paste with water, and rubbed through a fine sieve — that's how it's done."
"Smurov told me about your powder, only father says it's not real gunpowder," Ilusha said.
"Not real?" Kolya flushed. "It burns. I don't know, of course."
"No, I didn't mean that," the captain put in, looking guilty. "I only said real powder isn't made that way, but it doesn't matter — it can be made that way."

"I don't know, you'd know best. We lit some in a pomade jar, it burned beautifully, all burned away leaving just a tiny bit of ash. But that was only the paste, and if you rub it through ... well, you know best, I don't know.... And Bulkin's father thrashed him over our powder, did you hear?" he turned to Ilusha.
"Yes," Ilusha answered. He was listening to Kolya with intense interest and enjoyment.

"We'd made up a whole bottle of it and he kept it under his bed. His father found it. Said it might explode, and thrashed him on the spot. He was going to complain about me to the masters. He's not allowed to go around with me now — no one's allowed to go around with me now. Smurov isn't allowed to either — I've got a bad name with everyone. They say I'm a 'desperate character,'" Kolya smiled scornfully. "It all started with that business on the railway."

"Ah, we've heard about that exploit of yours, too," the captain cried. "How could you lie still on the track? Is it possible you weren't the least bit afraid, lying there under the train? Weren't you scared?"
The captain was abject in his flattery of Kolya.

"N—not especially," Kolya answered carelessly. "What's damaged my reputation around here more than anything was that cursed goose," he said, turning back to Ilusha. But though he kept up a careless air as he talked, he still couldn't help himself and kept losing the tone he was trying to hold.
"Ah! I heard about the goose!" Ilusha laughed, beaming all over. "They told me, but I didn't understand it. Did they really take you to court?"

"The most stupid, trivial business — they made a mountain out of a molehill, as they always do," Kolya began carelessly. "I was walking through the market square here one day, just as they'd driven in the geese. I stopped and looked at them. All at once a fellow — he's an errand boy at Plotnikov's now — looked at me and said, 'What are you looking at the geese for?' I looked at him; he was a stupid, moon-faced fellow of twenty. I'm always on the side of the peasantry, you know. I like talking to peasants.... We've fallen behind the peasants — that's an axiom. I believe you're laughing, Karamazov?"
"No, heaven forbid, I'm listening," said Alyosha, with such a good-natured air that the sensitive Kolya was reassured at once.

"My theory, Karamazov, is clear and simple," he hurried on, pleased with himself. "I believe in the common people and I'm always glad to give them their due, but I'm not for spoiling them — that's a _sine qua non_.... But I was telling you about the goose. So I turned to the fool and answered, 'I'm wondering what the goose is thinking about.' He looked at me quite blankly. 'And what is the goose thinking about?' he asked. 'You see that cart full of oats?' I said. 'The oats are spilling out of the sack, and the goose has stuck its neck right under the wheel to gobble them up — you see?' 'I see that well enough,' he said. 'Well,' I said, 'if that cart were to move on a little, would it break the goose's neck or not?' 'It'd break it for sure,' and he grinned all over his face, thoroughly delighted. 'Come on then,' I said, 'let's try it.' 'Let's,' he said. And it didn't take us long to arrange: he took hold of the bridle without being noticed, and I stood to one side to direct the goose. And the owner wasn't watching, he was talking to someone, so I had nothing to do — the goose stuck its head in after the oats on its own, under the cart, right under the wheel. I winked at the lad, he tugged the bridle, and crack. The goose's neck snapped clean in half. And, as luck would have it, all the peasants saw us right at that moment, and they raised a ruckus at once. 'You did that on purpose!' 'No, not on purpose.' 'Yes, you did, on purpose!' Well, they shouted, 'Take him to the justice of the peace!' They took me too. 'You were in on it too,' they said, 'you helped, everyone in the market knows you!' And, for some reason, I really am known all over the market," Kolya added, with some pride. "We all trooped off to the justice's, and they brought the goose along too. The fellow was crying, in a great panic, blubbering just like a woman. And the farmer kept shouting you could kill any number of geese that way. Well, of course, there were witnesses. The justice settled it in a minute: the farmer was to be paid a rouble for the goose, and the fellow got to keep the goose. And he was warned not to play tricks like that again. And the fellow kept blubbering like a woman. 'It wasn't me,' he said, 'he put me up to it,' and pointed at me. I answered, perfectly composed, that I hadn't put him up to anything, that I'd simply stated a general proposition, spoken hypothetically. The justice of the peace smiled, and then got annoyed at himself for smiling. 'I'll complain to your teachers about you, so that in future you won't waste your time on general propositions instead of sitting over your books and learning your lessons.' He never actually complained to the teachers — that was a joke — but the story got around and reached the teachers' ears anyway. They've got long ears, you know! The classical master, Kolbasnikov, was particularly scandalized by it, but Dardanelov got me off again. But Kolbasnikov's furious with everyone these days, like a green donkey. Did you know, Ilusha, he just got married, got a dowry of a thousand roubles, and his bride's an absolute fright, first-class, bottom of the barrel. The third-year fellows wrote an epigram about it:
Astounding news has reached the class, Kolbasnikov has been an ass.

And so on — it's awfully funny, I'll bring it to you later. I've got nothing against Dardanelov, he's a learned man, no doubt about that. I respect men like that, and it's not because he stood up for me."
"But you took him down over who founded Troy!" Smurov put in suddenly, plainly proud of Krassotkin at that moment. He'd especially loved the story of the goose.
"Did you really take him down?" the captain asked, in a flattering tone. "On the question of who founded Troy? We heard about it — Ilusha told me at the time."
"He knows everything, father, he knows more than any of us!" Ilusha put in. "He just pretends to be ordinary, but really he's top of the class in every subject...."
Ilusha looked at Kolya with boundless happiness.

"Oh, that's all nonsense about Troy, a trivial matter. I consider it an unimportant question," Kolya said, with haughty humility. He'd fully recovered his dignity by now, though he was still a little uneasy. He sensed he'd gotten quite worked up, and had talked about the goose, for instance, with too little restraint, while Alyosha had looked serious and hadn't said a word the whole time. And the vain boy was gradually starting to be gnawed by a fear that Alyosha's silence meant he despised him, thought he was showing off in front of him. If Alyosha dared think anything like that, Kolya would—
"I consider the question a perfectly trivial one," he said again, sharply, with pride.

"And I know who founded Troy," said a boy who hadn't spoken until then, to everyone's surprise. He'd been silent, apparently shy. He was a pretty boy of about eleven, named Kartashov. He sat near the door. Kolya looked at him with dignified astonishment.

The fact was, the identity of the founders of Troy had become a secret across the whole school, a secret that could only be uncovered by reading Smaragdov, and nobody had a copy of Smaragdov but Kolya. One day, while Kolya's back was turned, Kartashov had hastily opened Smaragdov, which lay among Kolya's books, and immediately hit upon the passage about the founding of Troy. This had happened quite a while before, but he'd felt uneasy and couldn't bring himself to announce publicly that he too knew who'd founded Troy, afraid of what might happen and of Krassotkin somehow shaming him over it. But now he couldn't resist saying it. He'd been longing to for weeks.

"Well, who did found it?" Kolya asked, turning to him with haughty condescension. He could see from his face that he really did know, and instantly decided how to handle it. There was, so to speak, a false note in the general harmony.

"Troy was founded by Teucer, Dardanus, Ilius, and Tros," the boy rattled off at once, and in the same instant blushed, blushed so hard it was painful to look at him. But the other boys stared at him — stared at him for a full minute — and then every eye swung at once toward Kolya, who was still studying the audacious boy with disdainful composure.
"In what sense did they found it?" he condescended to say at last. "And what exactly is meant by founding a city or a state? What did they do — do you suppose they each went and laid a brick?"
There was laughter. The offending boy went from pink to crimson. He said nothing, on the verge of tears. Kolya held him in suspense a minute longer.

"Before you talk about a historical event like the founding of a nation, you first need to understand what you even mean by it," he admonished him, in stern, incisive tones. "But I attach no importance to these old wives' tales, and I don't think much of world history in general," he added carelessly, addressing the whole room.
"World history?" the captain asked, looking almost frightened.

"Yes, world history! It's the study of humanity's successive follies, and nothing more. The only subjects I respect are mathematics and natural science," said Kolya. He was showing off, and he glanced at Alyosha; his was the only opinion he feared here. But Alyosha was still silent, still just as serious. If Alyosha had said one word, it would have stopped him — but Alyosha was silent, and "it might be the silence of contempt," which finally irritated Kolya.
"The classical languages too ... they're simply madness, nothing more. You seem to disagree with me again, Karamazov?"
"I don't agree," said Alyosha, with a faint smile.

"The study of the classics, if you want my opinion, is nothing but a police measure — that's the real reason it was introduced into our schools." Kolya was starting to run out of breath again. "Latin and Greek were brought in because they're deadly dull and they stupefy the mind. It was dull enough before, so what could they do to make things duller? It was senseless enough already, so what could they do to make it more senseless? So they came up with Greek and Latin. That's my opinion, and I hope I never change it," Kolya finished abruptly. His cheeks were flushed.
"That's true," Smurov agreed suddenly, in a ringing tone of conviction. He'd been listening carefully.
"And yet he's top of the class in Latin himself!" one of the boys cried out suddenly.
"Yes, father, he says that and he's still top in Latin," Ilusha echoed.

"What of it?" Kolya thought it necessary to defend himself, though the praise was very sweet to him. "I'm slogging away at Latin because I have to, because I promised my mother I'd pass my exams, and I think that whatever you do, it's worth doing well. But deep down I have a profound contempt for the classics and the whole fraud of it.... Don't you agree, Karamazov?"
"Why 'fraud'?" Alyosha smiled again.

"Well, all the classical authors have been translated into every language, so it wasn't for the sake of studying the classics that they brought in Latin, but purely as a police measure, to stupefy the mind. So what else can you call it but a fraud?"
"But who taught you all this?" Alyosha cried, genuinely surprised at last.

"First of all, I'm perfectly capable of thinking for myself, without being taught. Besides, what I just said about the classics being translated — our teacher Kolbasnikov said that to the whole of the third class."
"The doctor's here!" cried Nina, who'd been silent until then.

A carriage belonging to Madame Hohlakov pulled up at the gate. The captain, who'd been expecting the doctor all morning, dashed headlong out to meet him. "Mamma" pulled herself together and put on a dignified air. Alyosha went over to Ilusha and began straightening his pillows. Nina, from her invalid chair, watched anxiously as he tidied the bed. The boys hurriedly said their goodbyes. A few of them promised to come back that evening. Kolya called Perezvon and the dog jumped off the bed.
"I'm not leaving, I'm not leaving," Kolya said quickly to Ilusha. "I'll wait in the hallway and come back once the doctor's gone — I'll come back with Perezvon."

But by now the doctor had entered — an important-looking man with long dark whiskers and a shiny, clean-shaven chin, wearing a bearskin coat. As he crossed the threshold he stopped short, taken aback; he probably thought he'd come to the wrong place. "What's this? Where am I?" he muttered, not removing his coat or his peaked sealskin cap. The crowd, the poverty of the room, the washing hanging on a line in the corner, all threw him off. The captain, bent double, bowed low before him.
"It's here, sir, right here, sir," he muttered obsequiously; "it's here, you've come to the right place, you were on your way to us..."
"Sne-gi-ryov?" the doctor said loudly and pompously. "Mr. Snegiryov — is that you?"
"That's me, sir!"
"Ah!"

The doctor cast another squeamish glance around the room and threw off his coat, revealing the impressive decoration at his neck. The captain caught the fur coat in midair, and the doctor took off his cap.
"Where's the patient?" he asked, with emphasis.

title: VI. Precocity
paragraphs: "What do you think the doctor will say about him?" Kolya asked quickly. "What a repulsive mug he's got, though, hasn't he? I can't stand medicine!"
"Ilusha is dying. I think that's certain," Alyosha answered mournfully.
"They're rogues! Medicine's a fraud! I'm glad to have made your acquaintance, though, Karamazov. I've wanted to know you for a long time. I'm only sorry we're meeting under such sad circumstances."
Kolya badly wanted to say something even warmer, more heartfelt, but he felt awkward. Alyosha noticed, smiled, and pressed his hand.

"I've long since learned to respect you as someone out of the ordinary," Kolya muttered again, faltering and uncertain. "I've heard you're a mystic and that you were in the monastery. I know you're a mystic, but ... that hasn't put me off. Contact with real life will cure you of it.... It's always the way with characters like yours."
"What do you mean by mystic? Cure me of what?" Alyosha was rather taken aback.
"Oh, God and all the rest of it."
"What — don't you believe in God?"

"Oh, I've got nothing against God. Of course God's only a hypothesis, but ... I admit He's needed ... for the sake of order in the universe and all that ... and that if there were no God, He'd have to be invented," Kolya added, starting to blush. He suddenly worried Alyosha might think he was showing off his knowledge, trying to prove he was "grown up." "I haven't the slightest wish to show off my knowledge to him," Kolya thought indignantly. And all at once he felt terribly annoyed.

"I must confess I can't stand getting into discussions like this," he said, with an air of finality. "It's possible for someone who doesn't believe in God to love mankind, don't you think? Voltaire didn't believe in God, and he loved mankind?" ("There I go again," he thought to himself.)

"Voltaire did believe in God, though not very deeply, I think, and I don't believe he loved mankind very much either," Alyosha said quietly, gently, and quite naturally, as though speaking to someone his own age, or even older. Kolya was particularly struck by how tentative Alyosha seemed about his own opinion of Voltaire. He seemed to be leaving the question for him, little Kolya, to settle.
"Have you read Voltaire?" Alyosha finished.
"No, not exactly read.... But I read _Candide_, in the Russian translation ... a ridiculous, clumsy old translation ... (There I go again! Again!)"
"And did you understand it?"

"Oh, yes, all of it.... That is ... Why would you assume I wouldn't understand it? There's plenty of nastiness in it, of course.... Of course I understand that it's a philosophical novel, written to argue for an idea...." Kolya was starting to lose his footing. "I'm a Socialist, Karamazov, an incurable Socialist," he announced suddenly, apropos of nothing.
"A Socialist?" Alyosha laughed. "But when did you find the time to become one? I thought you were only thirteen?"
Kolya flinched.

"First of all, I'm not thirteen, I'm fourteen — fourteen in a fortnight," he flushed angrily, "and second, I'm completely at a loss to see what my age has to do with it. The question is what my convictions are, not what my age is, isn't it?"

"When you're older, you'll understand for yourself how age shapes convictions. And I had a feeling, too, that you weren't expressing your own ideas," Alyosha answered calmly and modestly, but Kolya broke in hotly:

"Come now, you want obedience and mysticism. You have to admit that the Christian religion, for instance, has only ever served the rich and powerful as a way to keep the lower classes in slavery. Isn't that so?"
"Ah, I know exactly where you read that, and I'm sure someone told it to you!" Alyosha cried.

"I say, what makes you think I read it somewhere? And certainly nobody told it to me. I can think for myself.... I've nothing against Christ, if you like. He was a deeply humane figure, and if He were alive today, He'd be found in the ranks of the revolutionaries, and would probably play a leading part.... There's no doubt about that."
"Oh, where, where did you get that from? What fool have you been keeping company with?" Alyosha exclaimed.
"Come, the truth will out! I'll admit I've often talked with Mr. Rakitin, of course, but ... old Byelinsky said it too, so they say."
"Byelinsky? I don't remember him writing that anywhere."
"If he didn't write it, they say he said it. I heard that from a ... but never mind."
"And have you read Byelinsky?"
"Well, no ... I haven't read all of him, but ... I read the part about Tatyana, about why she didn't go off with Onyegin."
"Didn't go off with Onyegin? Surely you don't ... understand that already?"

"Well, you seem to be taking me for little Smurov," Kolya said, with an irritated grin. "But please don't think I'm such a revolutionary. I often disagree with Mr. Rakitin. Though I bring up Tatyana, I'm not at all for the emancipation of women. I accept that women are a subject class and must obey. _Les femmes tricottent_, as Napoleon said." Kolya smiled, for some reason. "And on that question, at least, I'm entirely of one mind with that pseudo-great man. I also think that abandoning one's own country to run off to America is contemptible — worse than contemptible, foolish. Why go to America when there's so much good to be done for humanity right here? Especially now. There's a whole world of fruitful work waiting for us. That's what I told him."
"What do you mean? Told whom? Has someone already suggested you go to America?"

"I'll admit they've been after me to go, but I declined. That's strictly between us, of course, Karamazov — mind you, not a word to anyone. I only say this to you. I've no wish at all to fall into the clutches of the secret police and take lessons at the Chain Bridge.
Long will you remember The house at the Chain bridge.

Do you remember that one? It's splendid. Why are you laughing? You don't think I'm fibbing, do you?" ("What if he finds out I've only got that one issue of _The Bell_ in father's bookcase, and haven't read any more of it?" Kolya thought with a shudder.)

"Oh, no, I'm not laughing, and don't for a moment think I take you for a liar. No, indeed, I couldn't think that, because, alas, all of this is perfectly true. But tell me, have you read Pushkin — _Onyegin_, for instance? You mentioned Tatyana just now."
"No, I haven't read it yet, but I want to. I've got no prejudices, Karamazov — I want to hear both sides. Why do you ask?"
"Oh, no reason."

"Tell me, Karamazov, do you have an awful contempt for me?" Kolya suddenly rapped out, drawing himself up in front of Alyosha as though standing at drill. "Be so good as to tell me straight, without beating around the bush."
"I have contempt for you?" Alyosha looked at him, astonished. "What for? I'm only sad that a charming nature like yours should be twisted by all this crude nonsense before you've even begun living."
"Don't worry about my nature," Kolya broke in, not without some satisfaction. "But it's true I'm stupidly touchy, crudely touchy. You smiled just now, and I had the feeling you seemed to—"

"Oh, my smile meant something else entirely. I'll tell you why I smiled. Not long ago I read a piece of criticism by a German who'd lived in Russia, about our students and schoolboys today. 'Show a Russian schoolboy,' he writes, 'a map of the stars, something he knows nothing about, and he'll hand it back to you the next day with corrections.' No knowledge, and boundless conceit — that's what the German meant to say about the Russian schoolboy."

"Yes, that's exactly right," Kolya laughed suddenly, "exactly so! Bravo to the German! But he missed the good side of it, don't you think? Conceit, maybe — that comes with youth, and can be corrected if need be — but on the other hand there's an independent spirit almost from childhood, boldness of thought and conviction, and not the spirit of those sausage-makers, groveling before authority.... But the German was right all the same. Bravo, the German! Still, Germans ought to be strangled all the same. Even if they're good at science and learning, they still need strangling."
"Strangled — what for?" Alyosha smiled.

"Well, maybe I'm talking nonsense, I admit it. I'm awfully childish sometimes, and when I'm pleased about something I can't hold myself back and I'm ready to talk any amount of rubbish. But, I say, here we are chattering away about nothing, and the doctor's been in there a long time. But maybe he's examining mamma too, and that poor crippled Nina. I liked that Nina, you know. She whispered to me suddenly as I was leaving, 'Why didn't you come sooner?' And in such a voice, so reproachful! I think she's awfully sweet and pitiable."

"Yes, yes! Well, you'll be coming often, you'll see what she's like. It would do you a great deal of good to know people like that, to learn to value a great deal that you'll discover from knowing them," Alyosha said warmly. "That would do you more good than anything."
"Oh, how I regret, how I blame myself for not having come sooner!" Kolya exclaimed, with bitter feeling.
"Yes, it's a great pity. You saw for yourself how delighted the poor child was to see you. And how he ached for you to come!"

"Don't tell me! You're making it worse! But it serves me right. What kept me from coming was my conceit, my selfish vanity, and the wretched stubbornness I can never quite shake, though I've fought it my whole life. I see that now. I'm a beast in plenty of ways, Karamazov!"
"No, you have a charming nature, even if it's been twisted — and I quite understand why you've had such an influence on this generous, morbidly sensitive boy," Alyosha answered warmly.
"And you say that to me!" Kolya cried. "And would you believe it, I thought — I've thought several times since I got here — that you despised me! If only you knew how much I value your opinion!"
"But are you really so sensitive? At your age! Would you believe it — just now, while you were telling your story, I thought, watching you, that you must be very sensitive!"

"You thought that? What an eye you've got, I must say! I bet that was when I was talking about the goose. That was exactly when I imagined you had a great contempt for me for being in such a hurry to show off, and for a moment I actually hated you for it, and started babbling like a fool. Then I imagined — just now, right here — when I said that if there were no God He'd have to be invented, that I was in too much of a hurry to show off my knowledge, especially since I got that phrase out of a book. But I swear I wasn't showing off out of vanity — though I really don't know why. Because I was so pleased? Yes, I believe it was because I was so pleased ... though it's absolutely disgraceful for anyone to gush the moment they're pleased, I know that. But I'm convinced now that you don't despise me — it was all in my head. Oh, Karamazov, I'm profoundly unhappy. I sometimes imagine all sorts of things — that everyone's laughing at me, the whole world — and then I feel ready to overturn the whole order of things."
"And you make everyone around you miserable," Alyosha smiled.
"Yes, I make everyone around me miserable, especially my mother. Karamazov, tell me — am I very ridiculous right now?"

"Don't think about that, don't think about it at all!" Alyosha cried. "And what does ridiculous even mean? Isn't everyone constantly being, or seeming, ridiculous? Besides, nearly all clever people nowadays are terribly afraid of looking ridiculous, and that's what makes them unhappy. All that surprises me is that you'd feel that so early — though I've noticed it for some time, and not only in you. These days even children have started suffering from it. It's almost a kind of madness. The devil has taken the shape of that vanity and slipped into this whole generation; it's simply the devil," Alyosha added, without a trace of the smile Kolya, watching him, had expected to see. "You're like everyone else," Alyosha said, in conclusion, "that is, like a great many others. Only you mustn't be like everyone else — that's all."
"Even if everyone is like that?"

"Yes, even if everyone is like that. Be the one who isn't. You really aren't like everyone else — here you are, not ashamed to admit to something bad, even ridiculous. And who admits to that much these days? No one. People have even stopped feeling the urge to examine themselves. Don't be like everyone else, even if you're the only one who isn't."

"Wonderful! I wasn't wrong about you. You know how to give comfort. Oh, how I've longed to know you, Karamazov! I've been eager for this meeting a long time. Can you really have thought about me too? You said just now you'd thought of me too?"
"Yes, I'd heard of you and had thought about you too ... and if it's partly vanity that makes you ask, it doesn't matter."
"Do you know, Karamazov, this conversation of ours has been rather like a declaration of love," Kolya said, in a bashful, melting voice. "That's not ridiculous, is it?"
"Not at all ridiculous, and even if it were, it wouldn't matter, because it's been a good thing." Alyosha smiled brightly.
"But you know, Karamazov, you have to admit you're a little ashamed yourself right now.... I can see it in your eyes." Kolya smiled with a sly sort of happiness.
"Why ashamed?"
"Well, why are you blushing?"
"It's you who made me blush," Alyosha laughed, and he really did blush. "Oh, well, a little, heaven knows why, I don't know..." he muttered, nearly embarrassed.
"Oh, how I love and admire you at this moment, precisely because you're a little ashamed! Because you're just like me," Kolya cried, in real ecstasy. His cheeks glowed, his eyes shone.
"You know, Kolya, you're going to be very unhappy in your life," something made Alyosha say suddenly.
"I know, I know. How do you know it all in advance!" Kolya agreed at once.
"But you'll bless life on the whole, all the same."

"Exactly so, hurrah! You're a prophet. Oh, we'll get on well together, Karamazov! Do you know what delights me most? That you treat me completely as an equal. But we're not equals — no, we're not, you're better! But we'll get on. You know, all this last month I've been telling myself, 'Either we'll be friends at once, forever, or we'll part as enemies to the grave!'"
"And saying that, of course, you already loved me," Alyosha laughed cheerfully.
"I did. I loved you terribly. I've been loving you and dreaming about you. And how do you know it all in advance? Ah, here's the doctor. Goodness! What will he tell us? Look at his face!"

title: VII. Ilusha
paragraphs: The doctor came back out of the room, wrapped in his fur coat, cap on his head. His face looked almost angry and disgusted, as though he were afraid of getting dirty. He threw a cursory glance around the passage, looking sternly at Alyosha and Kolya as he did. Alyosha waved to the coachman from the door, and the carriage that had brought the doctor drove up. The captain darted out after the doctor and, bowing apologetically, stopped him to get one last word in. The poor man looked utterly crushed, a scared look in his eyes.

"Your Excellency, your Excellency ... is it really possible?" he began, but couldn't go on, and clasped his hands in despair. Still, he gazed at the doctor imploringly, as though a single word from him might yet change the poor boy's fate.
"I can't help it, I'm not God!" the doctor answered offhandedly, though with his usual air of importance.
"Doctor ... your Excellency ... and will it be soon, soon?"
"You must be prepared for anything," the doctor said, in sharp, emphatic tones, and, dropping his eyes, made to step out toward the carriage.
"Your Excellency, for Christ's sake!" the terrified captain stopped him again. "Your Excellency! But can nothing, absolutely nothing, save him now?"

"It's out of my hands now," the doctor said impatiently, "but h'm!..." he stopped suddenly. "If you could, for instance ... send ... your patient ... at once, without delay" (he spoke the words "at once, without delay" with an almost wrathful sternness that made the captain jump) "to Syracuse, the change to the new, be-ne-ficial climate might possibly bring about—"
"To Syracuse!" the captain cried, unable to grasp what he'd heard.
"Syracuse is in Sicily," Kolya suddenly cut in, by way of explanation. The doctor looked at him.
"Sicily! your Excellency," the captain faltered, "but you've seen" — he spread his hands, gesturing at his surroundings — "mamma and my family?"

"N—no, Sicily isn't the place for the family — the family should go to the Caucasus in early spring ... your daughter must go to the Caucasus, and your wife ... after a course of the waters in the Caucasus for her rheumatism ... must be sent straight to Paris, to the mental specialist Lepelletier — I could give you a note for him, and then ... there might be a change—"
"Doctor, doctor! But look!" The captain flung his hands wide again, in despair, indicating the bare wooden walls of the passage.
"Well, that's not my department," the doctor grinned. "I've only given you the answer medical science has to your question about possible treatment. As for the rest, to my regret—"

"Don't worry, apothecary, my dog won't bite you," Kolya rapped out loudly, noticing the doctor's rather uneasy glance at Perezvon, standing in the doorway. There was a note of anger in Kolya's voice. He used the word "apothecary" instead of "doctor" on purpose, and, as he explained afterward, used it "to insult him."
"What's that?" The doctor jerked his head up, staring at Kolya in surprise. "Who's this?" he asked Alyosha, as if expecting an explanation.
"It's Perezvon's master, don't worry about me," Kolya said, incisively again.
"Perezvon?" the doctor repeated, baffled.
"He hears the bell, but can't say where it is. Goodbye, we'll meet again in Syracuse."
"Who is this? Who is this?" the doctor flew into a towering rage.

"He's a schoolboy, doctor, a mischievous boy — pay him no mind," Alyosha said, frowning and speaking quickly. "Kolya, hold your tongue!" he cried at Krassotkin. "Pay him no mind, doctor," he repeated, somewhat impatiently.
"He wants a thrashing, a good thrashing!" the doctor stamped his foot in a fury.
"And you know, apothecary, my Perezvon might just bite!" Kolya said, turning pale, his voice trembling, his eyes flashing. "_Ici_, Perezvon!"
"Kolya, one more word out of you and I'll have nothing more to do with you," Alyosha cried, peremptory.
"There's only one man in the world who can give orders to Nikolay Krassotkin — this is the man," Kolya said, pointing to Alyosha. "I obey him — goodbye!"

He stepped forward, opened the door, and hurried into the inner room. Perezvon flew after him. The doctor stood frozen for five seconds in amazement, staring at Alyosha; then, cursing, he hurried out to the carriage, repeating aloud, "This is ... this is ... I don't know what this is!" The captain dashed forward to help him into the carriage. Alyosha followed Kolya back into the room. He was already at Ilusha's bedside. The sick boy was holding his hand and calling for his father. A minute later the captain came back too.

"Father, father, come ... we ..." Ilusha stammered, in violent excitement, but, unable to go on, he flung his wasted arms around his father and Kolya both, drawing them together into one embrace, hugging them as tightly as he could. The captain suddenly began shaking with silent sobs, and Kolya's lips and chin twitched.
"Father, father! How sorry I am for you!" Ilusha moaned bitterly.
"Ilusha ... darling ... the doctor said ... you'll be all right ... we'll be happy ... the doctor ..." the captain began.
"Ah, father! I know what the new doctor said to you about me.... I saw!" Ilusha cried, and again hugged them both with all his strength, hiding his face against his father's shoulder.
"Father, don't cry, and when I die, get a good boy, another one ... choose one of them all, a good one, call him Ilusha, and love him instead of me...."
"Hush, old man, you'll get well," Krassotkin suddenly cried out, in a voice that sounded angry.

"But never forget me, father," Ilusha went on, "come to my grave ... and, father, bury me by our big stone, where we used to go for walks, and come to me there in the evening, with Krassotkin ... and Perezvon.... I'll be expecting you.... Father, father!"
His voice broke. All three of them fell silent, still embracing. Nina was crying quietly in her chair, and at last, seeing everyone in tears, "mamma" too burst into tears.
"Ilusha! Ilusha!" she exclaimed.
Krassotkin suddenly freed himself from Ilusha's embrace.

"Goodbye, old man, mother's expecting me back for dinner," he said quickly. "What a shame I didn't tell her beforehand! She'll be dreadfully worried.... But after dinner I'll come back to you for the whole day, the whole evening, and I'll tell you all sorts of things, all sorts of things. And I'll bring Perezvon — but I'll take him with me now, because he'll start howling without me and bother you. Goodbye!"
And he ran out into the passage. He didn't want to cry, but out in the passage he burst into tears anyway. Alyosha found him crying.
"Kolya, you must keep your word and come, or he'll be terribly disappointed," Alyosha said firmly.
"I will! Oh, how I curse myself for not coming sooner!" Kolya muttered, crying, no longer ashamed of it.
At that moment the captain flew out of the room and at once shut the door behind him. His face looked frantic, his lips trembling. He stood before the two of them and flung up his arms.

"I don't want a good boy! I don't want another boy!" he muttered in a wild whisper, clenching his teeth. "If I forget thee, Jerusalem, may my tongue—" He broke off with a sob and sank to his knees before the wooden bench. Pressing his fists against his head, he began sobbing with absurd, whimpering cries, doing everything he could to keep the sound from reaching the room.
Kolya ran out into the street.
"Goodbye, Karamazov! Will you come yourself?" he called out sharply, almost angrily, to Alyosha.
"I will, certainly, this evening."
"What was that he said about Jerusalem?... What did he mean by that?"
"It's from the Bible. 'If I forget thee, Jerusalem' — that is, if I forget everything most precious to me, if I let anything take its place, then may—"
"I understand, that's enough! Mind you come! _Ici_, Perezvon!" he cried, with real ferocity, at the dog, and strode off home with rapid steps.

title: I. At Grushenka’s
paragraphs: Alyosha headed toward the cathedral square, to the widow Morozov's house, to see Grushenka, who'd sent Fenya to him early that morning with an urgent message begging him to come. Questioning Fenya, Alyosha learned that her mistress had been especially distressed since the day before. In the two months since Mitya's arrest, Alyosha had called often at the widow Morozov's house, both out of his own wish to and to carry messages for Mitya. Three days after Mitya's arrest, Grushenka fell seriously ill, and stayed ill for nearly five weeks. For an entire week she was unconscious. She'd changed a great deal — thinner, a bit sallow, though for the last fortnight she'd been well enough to go out. But to Alyosha her face seemed even more appealing than before, and he liked meeting her eyes whenever he came in to see her. A look of firmness, of intelligent purpose, had taken shape in her face. Signs of a spiritual transformation showed in her — a steadfast, fine, humble determination that nothing could shake. There was a small vertical line between her brows that gave her charming face a look of concentrated thought, almost stern at first glance. There was hardly a trace left of her old frivolity.

It struck Alyosha, too, as strange that despite the disaster that had befallen the poor girl — engaged to a man arrested for a terrible crime almost the instant of their engagement — despite her illness and the nearly inevitable sentence hanging over Mitya, Grushenka hadn't yet lost her youthful cheerfulness. A soft light had come into her once-proud eyes, though at times they still flashed with the old vindictive fire, whenever some disturbing thought stronger than ever gripped her heart. The object of that unease was the same as always — Katerina Ivanovna, whom Grushenka had even raved about while delirious with fever. Alyosha knew she was fiercely jealous of her. And yet Katerina Ivanovna had never once visited Mitya in prison, though she could have done so whenever she liked. All this made for a difficult problem for Alyosha, since he was the only person Grushenka opened her heart to, the only one she kept asking for advice. Sometimes he had no idea what to say.

Full of worry, he stepped into her lodging. She was home. She'd returned from seeing Mitya half an hour before, and from the quickness with which she leapt up from her chair to meet him he could see she'd been waiting for him impatiently. A deck of cards, dealt out for a game of "fools," lay on the table. A bed had been made up on the leather sofa on the other side, and Maximov lay half-reclining on it. He wore a dressing gown and a cotton nightcap, and was clearly ill and weak, though smiling blissfully. When the homeless old man had come back with Grushenka from Mokroe two months before, he'd simply stayed on, and was staying with her still. He'd arrived with her in rain and sleet, sat down on the sofa, soaked through and frightened, and gazed at her mutely with a timid, pleading smile. Grushenka, in terrible grief herself and in the first stage of fever, had almost forgotten he existed through all she had to see to that first half hour after her arrival. Then suddenly she happened to look at him closely: he gave a pitiful, helpless little laugh. She called Fenya and told her to bring him something to eat. He sat in the same spot all that day, almost without stirring. When it grew dark and the shutters were closed, Fenya asked her mistress:
"Is the gentleman staying the night, mistress?"
"Yes; make him a bed on the sofa," Grushenka answered.

Questioning him further, Grushenka learned from him that he had literally nowhere to go, and that "Mr. Kalganov, my benefactor, told me flat out that he wouldn't take me back, and gave me five roubles."

"Well, God bless you, you'd better stay then," Grushenka decided in her grief, smiling at him with pity. Her smile wrung the old man's heart, and his lips twitched with grateful tears. And so the destitute wanderer had stayed with her ever since. He didn't leave the house even while she was ill. Fenya and her grandmother, the cook, didn't turn him out, but kept serving him meals and making up his bed on the sofa. Grushenka had grown used to him, and coming back from seeing Mitya (whom she'd started visiting in prison even before she was really well) she'd sit down and start chatting with "Maximushka" about small things, to keep herself from dwelling on her sorrow. The old man turned out to be a fine storyteller on occasion, so that eventually he became necessary to her. Grushenka saw almost no one else besides Alyosha, who didn't come every day and never stayed long. Her old merchant lay gravely ill around this time, "at his last gasp," as they said in town, and he did in fact die a week after Mitya's trial. Three weeks before his death, sensing the end was near, he finally summoned his sons, their wives and children, up to his room, and told them not to leave him again. From that moment he gave strict orders to his servants not to let Grushenka in, and to tell her, if she came, "The master wishes you a long and happy life, and asks you to forget him." But Grushenka sent almost every day to ask after him.

"You've come at last!" she cried, flinging down the cards and greeting Alyosha joyfully. "And Maximushka's been scaring me, saying maybe you wouldn't come. Ah, how I need you! Sit down at the table. What'll you have — coffee?"
"Yes, please," said Alyosha, sitting down at the table. "I'm very hungry."

"That's right. Fenya, Fenya, coffee," Grushenka called. "It's been sitting ready for you a good while now. And bring some little pies, and mind they're hot. You know, we had quite a storm over these pies today. I took them to him in prison, and would you believe it, he threw them right back at me — wouldn't eat them. Flung one on the floor and stamped on it. So I told him: 'I'll leave them with the guard — if you haven't eaten them by evening, it'll mean your spite is all the food you need!' And with that I left. We quarreled again, would you believe it? Every time I go, we quarrel."
Grushenka said all this in one breath, agitated. Maximov, feeling nervous, smiled at once and looked down at the floor.
"What did you quarrel about this time?" Alyosha asked.

"I didn't expect it in the least. Just imagine — he's jealous of the Pole. 'Why are you keeping him around?' he said. 'So now you're keeping him too.' He's jealous, jealous of me all the time, jealous eating and sleeping! Last week he even got it into his head to be jealous of Kuzma."
"But he already knew about the Pole before?"

"Yes, but there it is. He's known about him from the very start, but today he suddenly sat up and started scolding me about him. I'm ashamed to repeat what he said. Silly man! Rakitin went in just as I was leaving. Maybe Rakitin's stirring him up. What do you think?" she added, carelessly.
"He loves you — that's what it is, he loves you so much. And right now he's especially on edge."

"I should think he would be, with the trial tomorrow. And I went to talk to him about tomorrow, because I dread even thinking what's going to happen then. You say he's on edge, but how on edge am I! And he goes on about the Pole! He's too silly! At least he's not jealous of Maximushka yet."
"My wife was dreadfully jealous over me too," Maximov put in.
"Jealous of you?" Grushenka couldn't help laughing. "Jealous of whom, over you?"
"Of the maidservants."

"Hush, Maximushka, I'm in no mood for laughing right now; I'm feeling angry. Don't ogle the pies — I'm not giving you any, they're not good for you, and I won't give you any vodka either. I have to look after him too, just as if I were running an almshouse," she laughed.
"I don't deserve your kindness. I'm a worthless creature," Maximov said, tears in his voice. "You'd do better to spend your kindness on people more useful than me."

"Oh, everyone has their use, Maximushka, and how are we to say who's most useful? If only that Pole didn't exist, Alyosha. He's taken it into his head to fall ill too, today, of all things. I went to see him as well. And I'll send him some pies too, just to spite Mitya. I hadn't sent him any before, but Mitya accused me of it, so now I will!Ah, here's Fenya with a letter! Yes, it's from the Poles — begging again!"

Pan Mussyalovitch had indeed sent an extremely long, characteristically flowery letter, begging her to lend him three roubles. Enclosed with the letter was a receipt for the sum, promising repayment within three months, signed by Pan Vrublevsky as well. Grushenka had received many such letters, each with its own receipt, from her former lover over the fortnight of her recovery. But she knew the two Poles had come to ask after her health while she was ill. The first letter she'd gotten from them was a long one, on large notepaper with a big family crest stamped on the seal. It was so obscure and overwrought that Grushenka set it down before she'd read even half, unable to make head or tail of it. She hadn't been up to reading letters then. That first letter was followed the next day by another, in which Pan Mussyalovitch begged her for a loan of two thousand roubles, for a very short term. Grushenka left that one unanswered too. A whole string of letters followed after that — one a day — every bit as pompous and overwrought, but the sum requested steadily shrank, dropping to a hundred roubles, then twenty-five, then ten, until finally Grushenka got a letter in which both Poles begged for just one rouble, with a receipt signed by both.

Then Grushenka suddenly felt sorry for them, and at dusk went round to their lodgings herself. She found the two Poles in real poverty, nearly destitute, without food or fuel, without cigarettes, in debt to their landlady. The two hundred roubles they'd carried off from Mitya at Mokroe had long since vanished. But Grushenka was startled to find them greeting her with arrogant dignity and self-importance, all punctilio and pompous speeches. Grushenka simply laughed, and gave her old admirer ten roubles. Then, laughing, she told Mitya about it, and he wasn't the least bit jealous. But ever since, the Poles had attached themselves to Grushenka and bombarded her daily with requests for money, and she'd always sent them small sums. And now, that very day, Mitya had suddenly gotten it into his head to be fiercely jealous.

"Like a fool, I stopped by his place for just a minute, on the way to see Mitya, because he's sick too, my Pole," Grushenka began again, with nervous haste. "I was laughing about it, telling Mitya. 'Fancy,' I said, 'my Pole took it into his head to sing me his old songs to the guitar. He thought I'd be so touched I'd marry him!' Mitya leapt up, swearing.... So there, I'll send them the pies! Fenya, is it that little girl they sent? Here, give her three roubles and wrap up a dozen pies in paper and tell her to take them. And you, Alyosha, be sure to tell Mitya I really did send them the pies."
"I wouldn't tell him for anything," Alyosha said, smiling.
"Ech! You think he's unhappy about it. Why, he's jealous on purpose. He doesn't actually care," Grushenka said bitterly.
"On purpose?" Alyosha asked.

"I tell you, you're being silly, Alyosha. For all your cleverness, you don't understand a thing about this. I'm not offended that he's jealous over a woman like me. I'd be offended if he weren't jealous. I'm like that. I don't take offense at jealousy. I've got a fierce heart myself. I can be jealous too. Only what offends me is that he doesn't love me at all. I tell you he's jealous now _on purpose_. Am I blind? Don't I see? He started talking to me just now about that woman, about Katerina, saying how she was this and that, how she'd sent for a doctor from Moscow for him, to try to save him, how she'd hired the best lawyer, the most learned one too. So he loves her — praising her to my face, more shame to him! He's treated me badly himself, so he attacked me, to make it look like I was to blame first, to throw the whole thing on me. 'You had your Pole before me, so I can't be blamed for Katerina' — that's what it amounts to. He wants to dump the whole blame on me. He attacked me on purpose, on purpose, I tell you, but I'll—"
Grushenka couldn't finish saying what she'd do. She buried her eyes in her handkerchief and sobbed violently.
"He doesn't love Katerina Ivanovna," Alyosha said firmly.

"Well, whether he loves her or not, I'll find out for myself soon enough," Grushenka said, with a menacing edge to her voice, pulling the handkerchief away from her eyes. Her face was distorted. Alyosha saw with sorrow that from being mild and serene, it had turned sullen and spiteful.

"Enough of this foolishness," she said suddenly. "It's not why I sent for you. Alyosha, darling, tomorrow — what's going to happen tomorrow? That's what's tormenting me! And it's only me it torments! I look at everyone and no one's even thinking about it. No one cares. Are you even thinking about it? He's tried tomorrow, you know. Tell me, how will he be tried? You know it was the valet, the valet who killed him! Good heavens! Can they convict him in the valet's place, with no one standing up for him? They haven't even bothered questioning the valet properly, have they?"

"He's been thoroughly cross-examined," Alyosha said thoughtfully; "but everyone concluded it wasn't him. He's very ill now, lying in bed. He's been ill ever since that attack. Truly ill," Alyosha added.
